To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts

Vasileios Saketos   William Réveillard11footnotemark: 1   Alexandre Proutière   Sebastian Dalleiger   Ming Xiao ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: KTH Royal Institute of Technology Affiliation: Stockholm, Sweden Email: {saketos,wilrev,alepro,sdall,mingx}@kth.se
Abstract

Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM’s answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose KL-PBD, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback–Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For KK confidence levels and horizon TT, KL-PBD achieves O⁡(K​log⁡T)O(K\log T) gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and O~​(K​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT}) worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where automated predictions can be complemented by human expertise, including customer support and healthcare (Huang et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025b; Bhattacharya et al., 2025). A natural design is to let the LLM handle routine queries while referring uncertain or high-risk cases to a human expert. Expert attention, however, is limited: reviewing a query takes time, and queries sent for review may have to wait behind previously deferred requests. Consequently, a deferral decision must account not only for whether the LLM is likely to be correct, but also for the congestion created by sending another query to the expert queue. Determining when the LLM is reliable is itself challenging: the correctness of a particular answer is not known unless a ground-truth label is obtained, which in our setting requires expert review. LLMs nevertheless provide signals that may be informative about their reliability: a prominent example is self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023), which measures agreement across multiple generated answers. Such signals can be correlated with correctness, but high confidence or agreement does not guarantee that the answer is correct (Aggarwal et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Thus, a deferral system must learn how the observed confidence signal relates to the probability that the LLM’s answer is correct.

We are interested in doing so online, without requiring a separate task-specific calibration dataset or retraining the LLM before deployment. Instead, the system learns from expert feedback generated during operation. This gives rise to a coupled learning-and-control problem with an unusual feedback structure. If the system accepts an LLM response, it observes no ground-truth label. If it defers, the label is revealed only after the query has been served by the expert. Feedback is therefore both selective and delayed. Moreover, acquiring information is itself costly: every deferred query consumes expert capacity, enters the queue, and may increase congestion for future queries. Deferral is therefore simultaneously a prediction decision, an information-acquisition decision, and a queue-control decision. We formalize this interaction as a finite-horizon online sequential decision problem. At each round, a query arrives together with the LLM’s answer and a confidence level, and the system decides whether to accept the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert queue. The conditional accuracy associated with each confidence level is initially unknown and must be learned from completed expert reviews. Our goal is to design an online policy that minimizes the expected cumulative cost over the horizon, balancing the risk of incorrect LLM answers, the congestion created by expert review, and the value of deferrals as a source of information for future decisions.

Our contributions are as follows.

(a) We propose KL-PBD, a queue-aware algorithm that learns the unknown conditional accuracies from delayed expert feedback. The algorithm acts optimally for a pessimistic estimate of the LLM’s reliability, favoring deferral, and hence information acquisition, when the available evidence is still limited, while explicitly accounting for the congestion cost of doing so.

(b) We establish near-optimal regret guarantees for KL-PBD. For KK confidence levels, the algorithm achieves O⁡(K​log⁡T/γ)O(K\log T/\gamma) regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is at least γ\gamma away from the deferral boundary, and O~​(K​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT}) regret in the worst case.

(c) We derive complementary lower bounds showing that logarithmic regret and inverse-gap dependence are unavoidable in separated instances, while the worst-case K​T\sqrt{KT} dependence is optimal up to logarithmic factors.

(d) We evaluate KL-PBD on synthetic and real-world question-answering tasks based on GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA. We demonstrate the importance of pessimism under selective feedback and show that explicitly accounting for the expert queue is paramount when expert service is congested (see Fig. 1 (right) for an illustrative example).

2 Related Work

Learning to defer.

Learning to defer studies systems that either make an automated prediction or delegate the decision to a human expert (Madras et al., 2018; Mozannar and Sontag, 2020). These foundational formulations jointly learn a predictor and a deferral rule, with subsequent work developing calibrated deferral objectives (Verma and Nalisnick, 2022). Post-hoc approaches instead learn when to defer the predictions of a fixed model (Narasimhan et al., 2022). These approaches are formulated as offline supervised learning problems, where the deferral policy is learned from a fixed labeled dataset and evaluated through test-time prediction risk. In our problem, the LLM response rule is fixed, but the system learns a deferral policy online from delayed, selectively observed human feedback generated by its own deferral decisions. Moreover, expert intervention is capacity constrained, making the cost of deferral state dependent rather than fixed. Further supervised and multi-expert formulations are discussed in Appendix D.3.

Online learning and selective feedback.

Reid et al. (2024) study online deferral under a total consultation budget. Their bandit feedback model reveals the reward of the selected action, including automated predictions. Online selective classification is closer to our setting: labels are observed only when the learner abstains from answering, and regret guarantees trade off prediction errors against selective label acquisition (Gangrade et al., 2021; Baharav et al., 2026). In our setting, labels are similarly observed only on deferrals, but a deferred query first enters the expert queue, and its label becomes available only once it has been served. Broader active-learning and oracle-query settings are discussed in Appendix D.6.

Deferral under limited review capacity.

Alves et al. (2024) consider cost-sensitive deferral to multiple experts under individual workload constraints, optimizing assignments using offline estimates of expert error. More directly related, Lykouris and Weng (2025) learn a binary classifier online while controlling admission to human review and scheduling; as in our model, feedback is selective and becomes available only after a review is completed. In this work, by contrast, the LLM response rule is fixed and the order of service is not controlled by the learner; what is learned is the LLM’s accuracy at each self-confidence level, which determines the deferral policy. Their benchmark allocates review capacity using expected arrival and service rates and assumes admitted jobs are reviewed immediately. We instead compare with the optimal finite-horizon policy subject to the same queue dynamics as the learner, with expert-review and holding costs included in the objective.

Additional related work on uncertainty signals and probabilistic calibration, LLM routing, structured admission-control policies, and human–AI decision support is discussed in Appendix D.

3 Problem formulation and optimal deferral

3.1 LLM–expert system model

We consider a sequential deferral problem over a known horizon TT. At each round t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T, a user query XtX_{t} may arrive. Upon receiving a query, the LLM produces a candidate answer RtR_{t} together with an index Jt∈[K]:={1,…,K}J_{t}\in[K]:=\{1,\ldots,K\}, which we call its self-confidence level. Our model is agnostic to how (Rt,Jt)(R_{t},J_{t}) is generated. A canonical example is self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023): the LLM generates K−1K-1 answers, RtR_{t} is chosen from the largest answer-equivalence class, and JtJ_{t} is one plus the size of that class, so that Jt=1J_{t}=1 when no answer can be extracted. Alternative constructions of (Rt,Jt)(R_{t},J_{t}) are discussed in Appendix D.1. Let Rt⋆R_{t}^{\star} denote the ground-truth answer and define Yt:=𝟏{Rt≡Rt⋆}Y_{t}:=\mathbf{1}\{R_{t}\equiv R_{t}^{\star}\}, where R1≡R2R_{1}\equiv R_{2} means that the two answers are equivalent. We set Jt=0J_{t}=0, Xt=Rt=∅X_{t}=R_{t}=\emptyset, Yt=1Y_{t}=1 when no query arrives and assume that (Jt,Yt)t≥1(J_{t},Y_{t})_{t\geq 1} is an i.i.d. sequence. For j∈[K]∪{0}j\in[K]\cup\{0\}, let ωj:=ℙ⁡(Jt=j)\omega_{j}:=\mathbb{P}(J_{t}=j), and for j∈[K]j\in[K], define11 1 If ωj=0\omega_{j}=0, hj⋆h_{j}^{\star} may be assigned arbitrarily. hj⋆:=ℙ⁡(Yt=1∣Jt=j)h_{j}^{\star}:=\mathbb{P}(Y_{t}=1\mid J_{t}=j). Thus, hj⋆h_{j}^{\star} is the LLM’s conditional accuracy at self-confidence level jj, and we call h⋆=(h1⋆,…,hK⋆)h^{\star}=(h_{1}^{\star},\ldots,h_{K}^{\star}) the conditional accuracy vector.

When a query arrives, the decision maker, who observes the self-confidence level JtJ_{t} but neither XtX_{t} nor RtR_{t}, either accepts the LLM answer or defers the query to a queue served by a pool of experts, who always provide the correct answer. We encode this decision by At∈{0,1}A_{t}\in\{0,1\}, where At=1A_{t}=1 denotes deferral. We set At=0A_{t}=0 if Jt=0J_{t}=0. Let BtB_{t} be the number of queries in the queue at the beginning of round tt, and let CtC_{t} be the number of queries that can be served by the experts between rounds tt and t+1t+1. We assume that (Ct)t≥1(C_{t})_{t\geq 1} is i.i.d. with distribution ρC\rho_{C} and independent of (Jt,Yt)t≥1(J_{t},Y_{t})_{t\geq 1} and the algorithm’s internal randomization, and that μ:=ℙ⁡(Ct≥1)>0\mu:=\mathbb{P}(C_{t}\geq 1)>0. The order in which pending queries are reviewed may depend on the observations and the service capacity, but not on unrevealed ground-truth labels. The queue is initially empty, B1=0B_{1}=0, and has known capacity B¯≥1\bar{B}\geq 1, so deferral is infeasible when Bt=B¯B_{t}=\bar{B}. Its dynamics are Bt+1=max⁡{0,Bt+At−Ct}B_{t+1}=\max\{0,B_{t}+A_{t}-C_{t}\}.

The cost incurred at round tt is ct:=chold​Bt+cexp​At+ce​(1−At)​(1−Yt)c_{t}:=c_{\mathrm{hold}}B_{t}+c_{\mathrm{exp}}A_{t}+c_{e}(1-A_{t})(1-Y_{t}), where chold≥0c_{\mathrm{hold}}\geq 0 is the per-round holding cost of each query in the queue, cexp≥0c_{\mathrm{exp}}\geq 0 is the cost of deferring a query to the experts, and ce>0c_{e}>0 is the cost of returning an incorrect LLM answer. At the end of the horizon, we account for the cost of serving the queries remaining in the queue. These cost parameters are known to the decision maker. Let D⁡(b)D(b) denote the expected holding cost of clearing a queue of size bb. It satisfies D⁡(0)=0D(0)=0 and, for b≥1b\geq 1, D⁡(b)=chold​b+𝔼C∼ρC​[D⁡((b−C)+)]D(b)=c_{\rm hold}b+\mathbb{E}_{C\sim\rho_{C}}\!\left[D\bigl((b-C)^{+}\bigr)\right]. The terminal cost is therefore D⁡(BT+1)D(B_{T+1}). For example, if C∼Bernoulli⁡(μ)C\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\mu), then D⁡(b)=chold​b​(b+1)/(2​μ)D(b)=c_{\rm hold}b(b+1)/(2\mu).

The resulting problem is a finite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP) with state (Bt,Jt)(B_{t},J_{t}), action AtA_{t}, per-round cost ctc_{t}, and terminal cost D⁡(BT+1)D(B_{T+1}). A policy π=(πt)t=1T\pi=(\pi_{t})_{t=1}^{T} is a sequence of possibly randomized decision rules, where πt\pi_{t} maps the current state (Bt,Jt)(B_{t},J_{t}) to a distribution over feasible actions. Our goal is to learn, online, a policy that performs nearly as well as the optimal policy that knows the conditional accuracy vector h⋆h^{\star}. We formalize this objective through regret after first characterizing the optimal policy under known h⋆h^{\star}.

3.2 Optimal deferral policy

Fix h∈[0,1]Kh\in[0,1]^{K} and set h0:=1h_{0}:=1. For j∈[K]∪{0}j\in[K]\cup\{0\}, define Lh​(j):=ce​(1−hj)L^{h}(j):=c_{e}(1-h_{j}), which, for j∈[K]j\in[K], is the expected error cost of accepting an LLM response with self-confidence level jj. Let VthV_{t}^{h} and QthQ_{t}^{h} denote the finite-horizon value and state-action value functions of the MDP induced by hh, with terminal value VT+1h​((b,j))=D⁡(b)V_{T+1}^{h}((b,j))=D(b). In other words, Qth​((b,j),a)Q_{t}^{h}((b,j),a) is the expected cost-to-go from state (b,j)(b,j) when action aa is taken at round tt, and Vth​((b,j))V_{t}^{h}((b,j)) is its minimum over feasible actions.

To simplify the notation, let Pa​(b,b′)P_{a}(b,b^{\prime}) denote the transition probability from queue state bb to b′b^{\prime} under action a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}. Since the queue dynamics depend on the current queue state and action, but not on the current self-confidence level, define, for b<B¯b<\bar{B},

Mth​(b):=cexp+∑b′=0B¯(P1​(b,b′)−P0​(b,b′))​∑j=0Kωj​Vt+1h​((b′,j)).M_{t}^{h}(b):=c_{\rm exp}+\sum_{b^{\prime}=0}^{\bar{B}}\bigl(P_{1}(b,b^{\prime})-P_{0}(b,b^{\prime})\bigr)\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}V_{t+1}^{h}((b^{\prime},j)). (1)

We refer to Mth​(b)M_{t}^{h}(b) as the marginal cost of deferral: it captures both the immediate expert-review cost and the expected increase in future cost caused by adding a query to the expert queue. We adopt the convention Mth​(B¯):=+∞M_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}):=+\infty.

For any b<B¯b<\bar{B} and j∈[K]j\in[K], the difference between the costs of deferring and accepting is

Qth​((b,j),1)−Qth​((b,j),0)=Mth​(b)−Lh​(j).Q_{t}^{h}((b,j),1)-Q_{t}^{h}((b,j),0)=M_{t}^{h}(b)-L^{h}(j).

Hence, the optimal decision compares the expected error cost of the LLM response with the marginal cost of deferral. The optimal policy has a threshold structure: a query is deferred whenever the LLM’s conditional accuracy is below a threshold determined by the current time and expert backlog. As stated in the following lemma, the threshold is endogenous: through Mth​(b)M_{t}^{h}(b), it accounts for the future congestion created by the current deferral decision.

Lemma 1 (Optimal deferral policy).

Fix h∈[0,1]Kh\in[0,1]^{K}. Resolving ties in favor of acceptance, an optimal action at round tt is Ath={Jt∈[K],Lh​(Jt)>Mth​(Bt)}A_{t}^{h}=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{J_{t}\in[K],\;L^{h}(J_{t})>M_{t}^{h}(B_{t})\right\}. Equivalently, defining the accuracy thresholds τth​(b):=1−Mth​(b)/ce\tau_{t}^{h}(b):=1-M_{t}^{h}(b)/c_{e}, for all b≤B¯b\leq\bar{B}, the optimal policy defers if and only if hJt<τth​(Bt)h_{J_{t}}<\tau_{t}^{h}(B_{t}). In particular, τth​(B¯)=−∞\tau_{t}^{h}(\bar{B})=-\infty, so deferral is infeasible when the queue is full.

3.3 Learning problem and regret decomposition

We now turn to the setting in which the true conditional accuracy vector h⋆h^{\star} is unknown. The statistical challenge is to learn h⋆h^{\star} while making deferral decisions. Feedback is both selective and delayed. If the learner accepts the LLM response (At=0A_{t}=0), its ground-truth label YtY_{t} is not revealed, and hence the corresponding error cost is not observed. If the learner defers (At=1A_{t}=1), the ground-truth label becomes available only once the query is processed by an expert. Thus, information about h⋆h^{\star} can be acquired only through the capacity-constrained experts, and the resulting feedback is delayed by the same queue that governs the deferral decisions. In particular, exploration affects not only the information available to the learner but also the future state of the system through congestion.

To isolate this learning challenge, our main analysis assumes that the distributions of the confidence levels ω\omega and of the service capacity ρC\rho_{C} are known. This assumption does not require analogous active exploration: the self-confidence level JtJ_{t} is observed whenever a query arrives, so ω\omega can be estimated passively from arrival frequencies, while observed service capacities provide samples from ρC\rho_{C} independently of the deferral decisions. In Appendix B.6, we extend our analysis to the setting where ω\omega and ρC\rho_{C} are unknown and show that our worst-case regret guarantees are preserved.

A learning algorithm π\pi is analogous to a policy, except that since it learns on the way, the decision taken at time tt may depend on all observations made until time tt. The expected regret of an algorithm π\pi is defined by:

RT​(π)=𝔼π​[∑t=1Tct+D⁡(BT+1)]−𝔼π⋆​[∑t=1Tct+D⁡(BT+1)].R_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}+D(B_{T+1})\right]-\mathbb{E}^{\pi^{\star}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}+D(B_{T+1})\right].

where π⋆\pi^{\star} is the optimal deferral policy for the conditional accuracy vector h⋆h^{\star}, identified in Lemma 1. Note that the oracle, applying π⋆\pi^{\star}, and the learner use the same KK self-confidence levels; hence, regret measures only the additional cost incurred from learning the unknown conditional accuracy vector h⋆h^{\star}, rather than any approximation error induced by the choice of confidence discretization.

For brevity, a superscript ⋆\star on a quantity denotes evaluation at h=h⋆h=h^{\star} (e.g. L⋆=Lh⋆L^{\star}=L^{h^{\star}}). Define the instantaneous decision gap Δt:=|L⋆(Jt)−Mt⋆(Bt)|𝟏{At≠At⋆}\Delta_{t}:=\bigl|L^{\star}(J_{t})-M_{t}^{\star}(B_{t})\bigr|\mathbf{1}\{A_{t}\neq A_{t}^{\star}\} when Jt∈[K]J_{t}\in[K] and Bt<B¯B_{t}<\bar{B}, and set Δt:=0\Delta_{t}:=0 otherwise.

Lemma 2 (Regret decomposition).

For any learning algorithm π\pi, RT​(π)=𝔼π​[∑t=1TΔt].R_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Delta_{t}\right].

Lemma 2 shows that regret is the expected cumulative decision gap over the rounds in which the learner takes a strictly suboptimal action. Consequently, the learning problem reduces to estimating h⋆h^{\star} accurately enough to identify on which side of the time- and backlog-dependent oracle threshold τt⋆​(Bt)\tau_{t}^{\star}(B_{t}) each self-confidence level lies.

4 The KL-PBD algorithm and its regret

4.1 Pessimistic Bellman deferral

We now introduce our algorithm KL-PBD, which learns the unknown conditional accuracy vector h⋆h^{\star} from delayed expert feedback while accounting for the congestion induced by deferral. KL-PBD is summarized in Algorithm 1.

For each self-confidence level j∈[K]j\in[K], let Nj,tN_{j,t} denote the number of level-jj queries whose expert reviews have been completed before the decision at round tt. Importantly, Nj,tN_{j,t} need not equal the number of level-jj queries deferred before tt: a deferred query contributes to Nj,tN_{j,t} only once it is served and its ground-truth label becomes available. The selective and delayed nature of the feedback thus enters the algorithm through Nj,tN_{j,t}. Let Yj,nY_{j,n} denote the label revealed by the nnth completed level-jj review, and, for n≥1n\geq 1, define h^j,n:=1n​∑ℓ=1nYj,ℓ.\widehat{h}_{j,n}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}Y_{j,\ell}. For T≥3T\geq 3, let ϕ⁡(T):=log⁡T+log⁡log⁡T\phi(T):=\log T+\log\log T denote the confidence budget. Given Nj,t≥1N_{j,t}\geq 1 observed labels, we form the KL lower confidence bound

h¯j,t:=inf{q∈[0,h^j,Nj,t]:Nj,t​kl⁡(h^j,Nj,t,q)≤ϕ⁡(T)}\underline{h}_{j,t}:=\inf\left\{q\in[0,\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}}]:N_{j,t}\,\operatorname{kl}\!\left(\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}},q\right)\leq\phi(T)\right\}

where kl\operatorname{kl} denotes the Bernoulli relative entropy, and set h¯j,t=0\underline{h}_{j,t}=0 when Nj,t=0N_{j,t}=0. At round tt, KL-PBD treats h¯t\underline{h}_{t} as the current conditional accuracy vector and applies the corresponding optimal policy (Algorithm 1, lines 5–6). Equivalently, the learner defers whenever the pessimistic expected error cost of the LLM exceeds the Bellman marginal cost of expert review.

In contrast, KL-PBD treats uncertain levels pessimistically: before sufficient expert feedback has accumulated, a smaller h¯j,t\underline{h}_{j,t} makes deferral more attractive and hence promotes the collection of additional labels. This exploration is nevertheless congestion-aware, since the decision is made through the threshold τ^t​(Bt)\widehat{\tau}_{t}(B_{t}) and therefore accounts for the current queue and the future cost of expert review.

4.2 Regret guarantees

We first give a gap-dependent regret guarantee. Recall that the oracle defers a level-jj query at state (t,b)(t,b) when hj⋆<τt⋆​(b)=1−Mt⋆​(b)/ceh_{j}^{\star}<\tau_{t}^{\star}(b)=1-M_{t}^{\star}(b)/c_{e}. The distance |hj⋆−τt⋆​(b)|\left|h_{j}^{\star}-\tau_{t}^{\star}(b)\right| therefore measures how far the conditional accuracy of level jj is from the oracle threshold at time tt and queue length bb. Equivalently, for b<B¯b<\bar{B}, |L⋆​(j)−Mt⋆​(b)|=ce​|hj⋆−τt⋆​(b)|\left|L^{\star}(j)-M_{t}^{\star}(b)\right|=c_{e}\left|h_{j}^{\star}-\tau_{t}^{\star}(b)\right| is the difference between the oracle QQ-values of accepting and deferring. Thus, the farther hj⋆h_{j}^{\star} is from the threshold, the less accurately it needs to be estimated to identify the oracle action.

Importantly, states at which hj⋆=τt⋆​(b)h_{j}^{\star}=\tau_{t}^{\star}(b) should not be treated as having a problematic “zero gap.” At such a state, L⋆​(j)=Mt⋆​(b)L^{\star}(j)=M_{t}^{\star}(b), so accepting and deferring have the same oracle QQ-value. Choosing either action therefore incurs no regret. Accordingly, the relevant notion of separation is the smallest nonzero distance from an oracle threshold. To formalize this, define the set of nonzero oracle gaps over the horizon by

𝒢T:={|hj⋆−τt⋆(b)|:j∈[K],t≤T,b<B¯,hj⋆≠τt⋆(b)}.\mathcal{G}_{T}:=\left\{\left|h_{j}^{\star}-\tau_{t}^{\star}(b)\right|:j\in[K],\;t\leq T,\;b<\bar{B},\;h_{j}^{\star}\neq\tau_{t}^{\star}(b)\right\}.

If 𝒢T=∅\mathcal{G}_{T}=\emptyset, every feasible oracle comparison is a tie. Hence the decision gap in Lemma 2 is zero at every round, and every algorithm has zero regret. We therefore restrict attention to the nontrivial case 𝒢T≠∅\mathcal{G}_{T}\neq\emptyset and define γT:=min⁡{1,min⁡𝒢T}\gamma_{T}:=\min\{1,\min\mathcal{G}_{T}\}. This quantity captures the smallest separation that the learner must resolve in order to distinguish a strict oracle preference between accepting and deferring. When this separation is bounded away from zero, sufficiently accurate estimates of h⋆h^{\star} identify the oracle action.

Theorem 1 (Gap-dependent regret of KL-PBD).

Suppose that 𝒢T≠∅\mathcal{G}_{T}\neq\emptyset. For every T≥3T\geq 3,

RT​(πKL-PBD)≤K​κ​ϕ​(T)+2​ce​∑j=1Kmin⁡{ωj​T,B¯+4​ϕ​(T)γT}+2​B¯​ce​[1+4​∑j=1Klog⁡(1+ωj​Tϕ⁡(T))]R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})\leq K\kappa\phi(T)+2c_{e}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\min\biggl\{\omega_{j}T,\bar{B}+\frac{4\phi(T)}{\gamma_{T}}\biggr\}+2\bar{B}c_{e}\biggl[1+4\sum_{j=1}^{K}\log\Bigl(1+\frac{\omega_{j}T}{\phi(T)}\Bigr)\biggr]

where κ:=4​e​(max⁡{ce,cexp}+chold​B¯/μ)\kappa:=4e(\max\{c_{e},c_{\mathrm{exp}}\}+c_{\mathrm{hold}}\bar{B}/\mu).

In particular, if γT≥γ>0\gamma_{T}\geq\gamma>0 uniformly in TT, then RT​(πKL-PBD)=O⁡(K​log⁡Tγ)R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})=O(\frac{K\log T}{\gamma}). Thus, when the conditional accuracies remain separated from the oracle thresholds, KL-PBD incurs only logarithmic regret. A stronger version of Theorem 1 is proven in Appendix B.4.

We next give a gap-free guarantee, which holds without any separation from the oracle thresholds. A stronger version of Theorem 2 is proven in Appendix B.3.

Theorem 2 (Worst-case regret of KL-PBD).

For every T≥3T\geq 3,

RT​(πKL-PBD)≤K​κ​ϕ​(T)+ce​∑j=1Kmin⁡{ωj​T,B¯+2​2​ωj​T​ϕ​(T)}+B¯​ce​[1+2​∑j=1Klog⁡(1+ωj​Tϕ⁡(T))].R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})\leq K\kappa\phi(T)+c_{e}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\min\biggl\{\omega_{j}T,\bar{B}+2\sqrt{2\omega_{j}T\phi(T)}\biggr\}+\bar{B}c_{e}\biggl[1+2\sum_{j=1}^{K}\log\Bigl(1+\tfrac{\omega_{j}T}{\phi(T)}\Bigr)\biggr].

Up to logarithmic factors, Theorem 2 gives RT​(πKL-PBD)=O~​(K+∑j=1Kmin⁡{ωj​T,ωj​T})R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})=\widetilde{O}(K+\sum_{j=1}^{K}\min\{\omega_{j}T,\sqrt{\omega_{j}T}\}). In particular, the worst case over arrival distributions yields O~​(K​T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT}) for K≤TK\leq T (Remark 1).

The main difficulty in the regret analysis is that h¯t\underline{h}_{t} also enters the marginal cost of deferral, so pessimism may cause KL-PBD not only to defer queries that the oracle accepts, but also to accept queries that the oracle defers. For a high-level summary of our proof technique, see Appendix B.1.

5 Lower bounds

We now show that the dependence on KK, TT, and the gaps in Theorems 1 and 2 is optimal in general (up to logarithmic factors for worst-case regret) by deriving matching lower bounds, which are proven in Appendix C. Write RT​(π,h)R_{T}(\pi;h) for the regret when the conditional accuracy vector is hh, and define τ:=1−[cexp+(1−μ)​chold/μ]/ce\tau:=1-[c_{\rm exp}+(1-\mu)c_{\rm hold}/\mu]/c_{e}. This is the largest accuracy threshold the oracle ever uses: τth​(b)≤τ\tau_{t}^{h}(b)\leq\tau for all hh, tt and bb, with equality at the empty queue in the last round (Lemma 18).

We first give an instance-dependent lower bound. We call an algorithm π\pi uniformly efficient if, run with horizon TT, it satisfies RT​(π,h)=o⁡(Tα)R_{T}(\pi;h)=o(T^{\alpha}) for every h∈[0,1]Kh\in[0,1]^{K} and every α>0\alpha>0. Let τ¯⋆:=limT−t→∞τt⋆​(0)\overline{\tau}^{\star}:=\lim_{T-t\to\infty}\tau_{t}^{\star}(0) be the long-horizon oracle threshold at the empty queue, which exists by Lemma 18. For every tt and bb, τt⋆​(b)≤τt⋆​(0)\tau_{t}^{\star}(b)\leq\tau_{t}^{\star}(0) (Proposition 1) and τ¯⋆≤τt⋆​(0)≤τ\overline{\tau}^{\star}\leq\tau_{t}^{\star}(0)\leq\tau (Lemma 18). Thus, τ¯⋆\overline{\tau}^{\star} is the long-horizon limit of the largest threshold the oracle uses.

Theorem 3 (Instance-dependent lower bound).

If τ¯⋆∈(0,1)\overline{\tau}^{\star}\in(0,1), every uniformly efficient algorithm π\pi satisfies

lim infT→∞RT​(π,h⋆)log⁡T≥ce∑j∈[K]:hj⋆>τ¯⋆,ωj>0hj⋆−τ¯⋆kl⁡(hj⋆,τ¯⋆).\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{R_{T}(\pi;h^{\star})}{\log T}\geq c_{e}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in[K]:\\ h_{j}^{\star}>\overline{\tau}^{\star},\ \omega_{j}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{h_{j}^{\star}-\overline{\tau}^{\star}}{\operatorname{kl}(h_{j}^{\star},\overline{\tau}^{\star})}. (2)

As the positive gaps hj⋆−τ¯⋆h_{j}^{\star}-\overline{\tau}^{\star} tend to zero, with τ¯⋆\overline{\tau}^{\star} bounded away from 00 and 11, each summand in the lower bound scales as 2​τ¯⋆​(1−τ¯⋆)/(hj⋆−τ¯⋆)2\overline{\tau}^{\star}(1-\overline{\tau}^{\star})/(h_{j}^{\star}-\overline{\tau}^{\star}). Hence, the logarithmic growth in TT and inverse-gap dependence of Theorem 1 are necessary in general. When μ=1\mu=1, τ¯⋆=τ\overline{\tau}^{\star}=\tau and KL-PBD attains equation 2 with equality (Proposition 3). Additionally, the stronger version of Theorem 1 proved in Appendix B.4 matches the dependence of Theorem 3 on the conditional accuracies for small gaps.

Our proof relies on a change-of-measure argument, as in Lai and Robbins (1985). The main difficulty in our setting is that the marginal cost of deferral depends on the round and the queue state, and that the oracle threshold changes with the instance. For a high-level summary of our proof technique, see Appendix C.1.

We next give a minimax lower bound.

Theorem 4 (Minimax lower bound).

Assume τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1). For every T≥1T\geq 1,

infπsuph∈[0,1]KRT​(π,h)≥1256​∑j=1Kmin⁡{μ3​ce​min⁡{τ,1−τ}​min​{ωj​T,ωj​T},μ2​chold​ωj​T}.\inf_{\pi}\sup_{h\in[0,1]^{K}}R_{T}(\pi;h)\geq\frac{1}{256}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\min\!\left\{\mu^{3}c_{e}\min\{\tau,1-\tau\}\min\{\omega_{j}T,\sqrt{\omega_{j}T}\},\ \mu^{2}c_{\rm hold}\,\omega_{j}T\right\}. (3)

When μ=1\mu=1, the last term can be dropped and the constant 1/2561/256 improved to 1/121/12.

If chold>0c_{\rm hold}>0 or μ=1\mu=1, the lower bound scales as ∑j=1Kmin⁡{ωj​T,ωj​T}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\min\{\omega_{j}T,\sqrt{\omega_{j}T}\}. Thus, its dependence on TT and ω\omega agrees with Theorem 2 up to logarithmic factors and the upper bound’s additive KK term. The lower bound is largest for balanced levels, ω0=0\omega_{0}=0 and ωj=1/K\omega_{j}=1/K (Remark 3), giving min⁡{T,K​T}\min\{T,\sqrt{KT}\} and matching the upper bound up to logarithmic factors for K≤TK\leq T.

The main difficulty in the minimax lower-bound construction is that hard instances cannot be obtained by perturbing the conditional accuracies around a fixed threshold, since the threshold itself depends on them, and that nearby instances are only guaranteed to have different optimal actions when the queue is empty. For a high-level summary of our proof technique, see Appendix C.1.

6 Numerical experiments

We now compare KL-PBD with baselines and examine the structure of the oracle policy on instances built from LLM outputs on GSM8K, NuminaMath-TIR and MedMCQA. Additional results and details are deferred to Appendices G and H.

Instances.

We use two LLMs, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-0.6B, and build one instance per dataset–LLM pair; results for Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct are reported in Appendix H. Each instance uses the self-consistency construction of Section 3: for every question, the LLM generates 2020 answers, so there are K=21K=21 levels. For a query at level jj, let pjp_{j} denote its self-consistency score, i.e., the fraction of generated answers that agree with RtR_{t}, so that p=(p1,…,pK)=(0,.05,…,1)p=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{K})=(0,.05,\ldots,1), where p1=0p_{1}=0 corresponds to queries for which no answer could be extracted. We take ωj\omega_{j} and hj⋆h_{j}^{\star} to be the empirical frequency and conditional accuracy of self-consistency level jj over the whole dataset, and sample queries independently with replacement from that dataset, so that a query arrives at every round (ω0=0\omega_{0}=0). Regret is evaluated against the optimal policy for this empirical instance. Figure 2 shows three calibration regimes. On GSM8K and NuminaMath the score is informative: Qwen3-0.6B is especially close to calibrated on GSM8K, while Qwen3-4B is underconfident at low scores and overconfident at high scores. On MedMCQA, the score is nearly uninformative: accuracy barely varies with the score below 100%100\%, and the 100%100\% level has accuracy only .79.79 (Qwen3-4B) and .68.68 (Qwen3-0.6B).

Setup and baselines.

We set (ce,cexp,chold)=(1,0.25,0.03)(c_{e},c_{\rm exp},c_{\rm hold})=(1,0.25,0.03), B¯=8\bar{B}=8, Ct∼Bernoulli⁡(0.35)C_{t}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.35), and T=105T=10^{5}. The arrival distribution ω\omega is unknown to the algorithms and is estimated as ω^j,t=t−1∑s=1t𝟏{Js=j}\hat{\omega}_{j,t}=t^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\mathbf{1}\{J_{s}=j\} by all methods that require it, except FQT, which is tuned under a uniform ω\omega. We compare KL-PBD with: i) SALMUT-SF, a threshold-based actor–critic policy adapted from Roy et al. (2021) to handle unknown rewards and selective feedback; ii) Fixed Queue Threshold (FQT), a non-learning baseline that uses a queue threshold optimized under the surrogate h=ph=p; iii) variants of KL-PBD, namely KL-PBD+, which uses a more aggressive confidence budget inspired by KL-UCB+ type rules (Garivier and Cappé, 2011; Achab et al., 2018), Greedy Bellman Deferral (GBD), which replaces the lower confidence bound h¯t\underline{h}_{t} by the empirical mean h^j,Nj,t\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}}, and Naive Bellman Deferral (NBD), which freezes the estimate at h=ph=p, i.e., treats the score as calibrated. These baselines are described in more detail in Appendix F.

Regret of KL-PBD against baselines.

In Figure 3, we report regret averaged over 100100 independent runs with pointwise 95%95\% confidence bands. Solid lines are algorithms that learn h⋆h^{\star}, and dashed lines are the baselines using the h=ph=p surrogate. The results illustrate the impact of score calibration: on GSM8K and NuminaMath, NBD is generally the best non-learning baseline and competes with KL-PBD over this horizon, whereas on MedMCQA it incurs 2020 to 6565 times the regret of KL-PBD+. Among learning algorithms, GBD suffers from the selective-feedback failure described in Appendix H.5, and SALMUT-SF adapts too slowly to be competitive. KL-PBD+ attains the lowest regret in all six instances, up to a factor 44 below KL-PBD: its more aggressive level-dependent confidence budget reduces the conservatism of the deferral rule. Appendix H reports regret values at horizons T∈{104,5⋅104,105,2⋅105}T\in\{10^{4},5\cdot 10^{4},10^{5},2\cdot 10^{5}\}; the gap between KL-PBD+ and the h=ph=p baselines keeps widening with TT. Comparisons to queue-unaware baselines, including adaptations of bandit algorithms from Achab et al. (2018), are deferred to Appendix H.3: KL-PBD and KL-PBD+ generally beat them by a wide margin when μ<1\mu<1, and remain competitive under immediate service (μ=1\mu=1).

Structure of the oracle policy.

Figure 4 shows the oracle threshold and the resulting decisions for Qwen3-0.6B. For every μ\mu, the threshold decreases with the queue state, as established in Proposition 1. Higher values of μ\mu lead to higher deferral thresholds, as faster expert service reduces the congestion cost of deferral: the oracle then defers even queries on which the LLM is fairly accurate. The bottom row shows the oracle deferral decisions for the service rate μ=0.35\mu=0.35 used in the regret experiments. Accordingly, the oracle defers fewer levels as the queue becomes more congested. In contrast, it does not always defer fewer levels as self-consistency increases: since the oracle defers exactly the levels whose conditional accuracy lies below the threshold, this occurs because the conditional accuracy is non-monotone and the threshold falls between the accuracies of two levels whose order is reversed relative to their self-consistency. Similar plots for Qwen3-4B and comparisons with the thresholds and decisions learned by KL-PBD are deferred to Appendix H.4.

7 Conclusion

We studied online deferral to a congested expert, where deferral costs depend on the queue state and expert feedback is both selective and delayed. This creates a feedback loop: learning when to trust the LLM requires expert labels, but acquiring those labels consumes the same limited resource that the learner is trying to manage. KL-PBD addresses this through pessimistic estimates of the unknown conditional accuracies, preventing premature acceptance from cutting off the feedback needed for learning. Its regret guarantees are near-optimal in both the worst-case and gap-dependent regimes.

Several extensions are natural. First, expert effort could depend on the query: low-confidence queries may also be harder to review, making service times confidence-level dependent. Second, our benchmark fixes a discretization of the confidence score; for continuous scores especially, choosing the number of levels would trade approximation error against statistical complexity. Third, the number of LLM generations could itself be treated as a design variable, trading the quality of the confidence signal against inference cost.

AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with: i) writing and editing, and in particular, to improve the presentation of the proofs; ii) coding, to help implement our algorithms and write data-processing and parsing scripts; iii) literature search, to help identify potentially relevant work.

The coding assistance was used strictly to implement our ideas and methods. We conducted our own literature review, and AI was used as a complementary tool for discovering potentially relevant references that we might have missed, not for synthesizing the literature on our behalf. We checked and revised all AI-assisted text and code, and independently verified all AI-suggested references and literature-related claims against the original sources. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work.

Reproducibility statement

We provide a complete description of our problem setting and assumptions in Section 3, and of our algorithm in Section 4. Full proofs of our results are given in Appendices A–C, with accompanying proof sketches to help the reader navigate them. Our experimental setup is described in Section 6 and Appendices E–H, including the datasets used and how they were parsed, the baselines we compare our algorithm to, and our evaluation protocol. The code used to reproduce our experiments is included in the supplementary material.

Appendix Content

Appendix A Proofs for Section 3

Throughout the appendices, write ℬ:={0,…,B¯}\mathcal{B}:=\{0,\ldots,\bar{B}\} and St:=(Bt,Jt)S_{t}:=(B_{t},J_{t}). Let 𝒜⁡(b,j):={0,1}\mathcal{A}(b,j):=\{0,1\} when j∈[K]j\in[K] and b<B¯b<\bar{B}, and 𝒜⁡(b,j):={0}\mathcal{A}(b,j):=\{0\} otherwise. We recall that action 11 corresponds to deferral, and action 00 to acceptance. Let ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} be the sigma-field generated by the self-confidence levels, actions, service capacities, completed-query identities and their revealed ground-truth labels through the end of round tt, together with past internal randomization. The algorithm chooses AtA_{t} using only ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}, JtJ_{t}, and independent randomization. The queries completed in each round are selected using only the observed history and service capacity, before any of their ground-truth labels are revealed. Thus BtB_{t} is ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}-measurable, whereas JtJ_{t} is independent of ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} with distribution ω\omega. For a real-valued function ff on a finite domain, we write sp⁡(f):=maxx⁡f⁡(x)−minx⁡f⁡(x)\operatorname{sp}(f):=\max_{x}f(x)-\min_{x}f(x).

A.1 Optimal deferral and regret decomposition

Proof of Lemma 1.

For b<B¯b<\bar{B}, j∈[K]j\in[K], and s=(b,j)s=(b,j),

Qth​(s,1)−Qth​(s,0)=Mth​(b)−Lh​(j).Q_{t}^{h}(s,1)-Q_{t}^{h}(s,0)=M_{t}^{h}(b)-L^{h}(j). (4)

Hence deferral is optimal when Lh​(j)>Mth​(b)L^{h}(j)>M_{t}^{h}(b), acceptance is optimal when Lh​(j)<Mth​(b)L^{h}(j)<M_{t}^{h}(b), and both actions are optimal at equality. On no-query and full-queue states, acceptance is the only feasible action. Resolving ties in favor of acceptance gives the stated action rule and its equivalent threshold formulation. ∎

Proof of Lemma 2.

All expectations are under the true conditional accuracy vector h⋆h^{\star}. By the Bellman definition and the observation model,

Qt⋆(St,At)=𝔼π[ct+Vt+1⋆(St+1)∣ℱt−1,Jt,At].Q_{t}^{\star}(S_{t},A_{t})=\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\!\left[c_{t}+V_{t+1}^{\star}(S_{t+1})\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},J_{t},A_{t}\right].

Taking expectations and summing over tt, the value terms telescope:

𝔼π​[∑t=1T(Qt⋆​(St,At)−Vt⋆​(St))]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(Q_{t}^{\star}(S_{t},A_{t})-V_{t}^{\star}(S_{t})\bigr)\right]={} 𝔼π​[∑t=1Tct+D⁡(BT+1)]−𝔼π​[V1⋆​(S1)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}+D(B_{T+1})\right]-\mathbb{E}^{\pi}[V_{1}^{\star}(S_{1})].

Since B1=0B_{1}=0 and J1∼ωJ_{1}\sim\omega under both the algorithm and the oracle policy,

𝔼π​[V1⋆​(S1)]=∑j=0Kωj​V1⋆​((0,j))=𝔼π⋆​[∑t=1Tct+D⁡(BT+1)].\mathbb{E}^{\pi}[V_{1}^{\star}(S_{1})]=\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}V_{1}^{\star}((0,j))=\mathbb{E}^{\pi^{\star}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}+D(B_{T+1})\right].

Consequently,

RT​(π)=𝔼π​[∑t=1T(Qt⋆​(St,At)−Vt⋆​(St))].R_{T}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(Q_{t}^{\star}(S_{t},A_{t})-V_{t}^{\star}(S_{t})\bigr)\right]. (5)

When Jt∈[K]J_{t}\in[K] and Bt<B¯B_{t}<\bar{B}, equation 4 gives

Qt⋆(St,At)−Vt⋆(St)=|L⋆(Jt)−Mt⋆(Bt)|𝟏{At≠At⋆}=ΔtQ_{t}^{\star}(S_{t},A_{t})-V_{t}^{\star}(S_{t})=\bigl|L^{\star}(J_{t})-M_{t}^{\star}(B_{t})\bigr|\mathbf{1}\{A_{t}\neq A_{t}^{\star}\}=\Delta_{t}

since the action space is binary. Otherwise, acceptance is the only feasible action, and both sides are zero. Substitution into equation 5 proves the claim. ∎

A.2 Service-capacity structure

In this section, we prove several structural properties induced by our service-capacity model. The proposition below states that the marginal cost of deferral increases with the expert queue state.

Proposition 1 (Monotone marginal cost).

For every conditional accuracy vector hh and every t≤Tt\leq T, the Bellman marginal cost is nondecreasing in the queue state:

cexp≤Mth​(0)≤Mth​(1)≤⋯≤Mth​(B¯−1).c_{\mathrm{exp}}\leq M_{t}^{h}(0)\leq M_{t}^{h}(1)\leq\cdots\leq M_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1).

Consequently, for every round tt and self-confidence level j∈[K]j\in[K], there exists a threshold τt,jqueue​(h)∈{0,…,B¯}\tau_{t,j}^{\rm queue}(h)\in\{0,\ldots,\bar{B}\} such that, resolving ties in favor of acceptance, the optimal policy defers a query with self-confidence level jj if and only if

Bt<τt,jqueue​(h).B_{t}<\tau_{t,j}^{\rm queue}(h).

For a conditional accuracy vector hh, consider the queue value

Uth​(b):=∑j=0Kωj​Vth​((b,j)),U_{t}^{h}(b):=\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}V_{t}^{h}((b,j)),

i.e., the value at queue state bb before the level of the incoming query is revealed. For t≤Tt\leq T and b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B}, let Fth​(b):=𝔼⁡[Ut+1h​((b−Ct)+)]F_{t}^{h}(b):=\mathbb{E}[U_{t+1}^{h}((b-C_{t})^{+})], and, for b<B¯b<\bar{B}, define dth​(b):=Fth​(b+1)−Fth​(b)d_{t}^{h}(b):=F_{t}^{h}(b+1)-F_{t}^{h}(b). Then the Bellman marginal cost can be written as

Mth​(b)=cexp+dth​(b),b<B¯.M_{t}^{h}(b)=c_{\mathrm{exp}}+d_{t}^{h}(b),\qquad b<\bar{B}. (6)

We first establish the structural properties of the queue value function that will also be useful later. Define its adjacent increments by

xth(q):=Uth(q)−Uth(q−1),q=1,…,B¯.x_{t}^{h}(q):=U_{t}^{h}(q)-U_{t}^{h}(q-1),\qquad q=1,\ldots,\bar{B}.
Lemma 3 (Queue-value increments under service capacity).

For every conditional accuracy vector hh and every t≤T+1t\leq T+1,

0≤xth​(1)≤xth​(2)≤⋯≤xth​(B¯).0\leq x_{t}^{h}(1)\leq x_{t}^{h}(2)\leq\cdots\leq x_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}).

Consequently, UthU_{t}^{h} is nondecreasing and discrete convex in the queue state.

Moreover, for every t≤Tt\leq T and b<B¯b<\bar{B},

dth​(b)=∑c=0bρC​(c)​xt+1h​(b+1−c).d_{t}^{h}(b)=\sum_{c=0}^{b}\rho_{C}(c)\,x_{t+1}^{h}(b+1-c). (7)
Proof.

Equation 7 follows directly from the service-capacity dynamics. Indeed,

dth​(b)=𝔼⁡[Ut+1h​((b+1−Ct)+)−Ut+1h​((b−Ct)+)].d_{t}^{h}(b)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[U_{t+1}^{h}((b+1-C_{t})^{+})-U_{t+1}^{h}((b-C_{t})^{+})\right].

If Ct=c≤bC_{t}=c\leq b, the two queue states differ by one and the difference equals xt+1h​(b+1−c)x_{t+1}^{h}(b+1-c). If c>bc>b, both queue states are zero. Hence equation 7 follows.

We prove the monotonicity of the increments by backward induction. At t=T+1t=T+1, we have UT+1h=DU_{T+1}^{h}=D, independently of hh. Let S0:=0S_{0}:=0 and Sk:=C1+⋯+CkS_{k}:=C_{1}+\cdots+C_{k} for k≥1k\geq 1, where C1,C2,…C_{1},C_{2},\ldots are i.i.d. with law ρC\rho_{C}. Iterating the definition of DD gives

D⁡(b)=chold​∑k≥0𝔼⁡[(b−Sk)+].D(b)=c_{\rm hold}\sum_{k\geq 0}\mathbb{E}[(b-S_{k})^{+}].

The series is finite since μ>0\mu>0. Let g⁡(q):=D⁡(q)−D⁡(q−1)g(q):=D(q)-D(q-1). Since (q−Sk)+−(q−1−Sk)+=𝟏{Sk<q},(q-S_{k})^{+}-(q-1-S_{k})^{+}=\mathbf{1}\{S_{k}<q\}, we have

g⁡(q)=chold​∑k≥0ℙ⁡(Sk<q).g(q)=c_{\rm hold}\sum_{k\geq 0}\mathbb{P}(S_{k}<q).

Thus g⁡(q)≥0g(q)\geq 0 and is nondecreasing in qq, so

0≤g⁡(1)≤g⁡(2)≤⋯≤g⁡(B¯).0\leq g(1)\leq g(2)\leq\cdots\leq g(\bar{B}).

Therefore UT+1h=DU_{T+1}^{h}=D is nondecreasing and discrete convex, establishing the base case.

Suppose now that

0≤xt+1h​(1)≤⋯≤xt+1h​(B¯).0\leq x_{t+1}^{h}(1)\leq\cdots\leq x_{t+1}^{h}(\bar{B}).

Equation 7 immediately gives dth​(b)≥0d_{t}^{h}(b)\geq 0. Moreover, for b<B¯−1b<\bar{B}-1,

dth​(b+1)−dth​(b)=\displaystyle d_{t}^{h}(b+1)-d_{t}^{h}(b)={} ∑c=0bρC​(c)​[xt+1h​(b+2−c)−xt+1h​(b+1−c)]\displaystyle\sum_{c=0}^{b}\rho_{C}(c)\left[x_{t+1}^{h}(b+2-c)-x_{t+1}^{h}(b+1-c)\right]
+ρC​(b+1)​xt+1h​(1)≥0.\displaystyle+\rho_{C}(b+1)x_{t+1}^{h}(1)\geq 0.

Thus

0≤dth​(0)≤dth​(1)≤⋯≤dth​(B¯−1).0\leq d_{t}^{h}(0)\leq d_{t}^{h}(1)\leq\cdots\leq d_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1). (8)

For j=0,…,Kj=0,\ldots,K, write rjh:=Lh​(j)−cexp.r_{j}^{h}:=L^{h}(j)-c_{\mathrm{exp}}. In particular, r0h=−cexpr_{0}^{h}=-c_{\mathrm{exp}} because Lh​(0)=0L^{h}(0)=0.

For b<B¯b<\bar{B}, the Bellman equation for the queue value function gives

Uth​(b)=chold​b+Fth​(b)+cexp+∑j=0Kωj​min⁡{rjh,dth​(b)}.U_{t}^{h}(b)=c_{\mathrm{hold}}b+F_{t}^{h}(b)+c_{\mathrm{exp}}+\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}\min\{r_{j}^{h},d_{t}^{h}(b)\}.

Indeed, for j∈[K]j\in[K] this represents the minimum between acceptance and deferral costs. For j=0j=0, action 00 is forced; since r0h=−cexpr_{0}^{h}=-c_{\mathrm{exp}} and dth​(b)≥0d_{t}^{h}(b)\geq 0, the corresponding term satisfies cexp+min⁡{r0h,dth​(b)}=0c_{\mathrm{exp}}+\min\{r_{0}^{h},d_{t}^{h}(b)\}=0, and therefore represents the no-query state correctly.

Consequently, for 1≤q<B¯1\leq q<\bar{B}, subtracting the Bellman equations for the queue value function at qq and q−1q-1 gives

xth​(q)=\displaystyle x_{t}^{h}(q)={} chold+dth​(q−1)+∑j=0Kωj​[min⁡{rjh,dth​(q)}−min⁡{rjh,dth​(q−1)}]\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{hold}}+d_{t}^{h}(q-1)+\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}\left[\min\{r_{j}^{h},d_{t}^{h}(q)\}-\min\{r_{j}^{h},d_{t}^{h}(q-1)\}\right] (9)
=\displaystyle={} chold+∑j=0Kωj​med⁡{dth​(q−1),dth​(q),rjh},\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{hold}}+\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}\operatorname{med}\{d_{t}^{h}(q-1),d_{t}^{h}(q),r_{j}^{h}\},

where the second equality uses ∑j=0Kωj=1\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}=1 and dth​(q−1)≤dth​(q)d_{t}^{h}(q-1)\leq d_{t}^{h}(q), and med⁡{x,y,z}\operatorname{med}\{x,y,z\} denotes the median of its three arguments.

At q=B¯q=\bar{B}, action 11 is infeasible. Hence

Uth​(B¯)=chold​B¯+Fth​(B¯)+∑j=0Kωj​Lh​(j),U_{t}^{h}(\bar{B})=c_{\mathrm{hold}}\bar{B}+F_{t}^{h}(\bar{B})+\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}L^{h}(j),

which together with the Bellman equation at B¯−1\bar{B}-1 yields

xth​(B¯)=chold+∑j=0Kωj​max⁡{dth​(B¯−1),rjh}.x_{t}^{h}(\bar{B})=c_{\mathrm{hold}}+\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}\max\left\{d_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1),r_{j}^{h}\right\}. (10)

By equation 8, for every fixed rr, med⁡{dth​(q−1),dth​(q),r}\operatorname{med}\{d_{t}^{h}(q-1),d_{t}^{h}(q),r\} is nonnegative and nondecreasing in qq. Therefore

0≤xth​(1)≤⋯≤xth​(B¯−1).0\leq x_{t}^{h}(1)\leq\cdots\leq x_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1).

Finally,

max⁡{dth​(B¯−1),r}≥med⁡{dth​(B¯−2),dth​(B¯−1),r},\max\left\{d_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1),r\right\}\geq\operatorname{med}\left\{d_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-2),d_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1),r\right\},

whenever B¯≥2\bar{B}\geq 2. Combining equation 9 and equation 10 therefore gives xth​(B¯)≥xth​(B¯−1)x_{t}^{h}(\bar{B})\geq x_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1). For B¯=1\bar{B}=1, the conclusion follows directly from equation 10. This completes the backward induction. ∎

Proof of Proposition 1.

By Lemma 3, xt+1h​(q)x_{t+1}^{h}(q) is nonnegative and nondecreasing in qq. Hence equation 7 and equation 6 give

0≤dth​(0)≤dth​(1)≤⋯≤dth​(B¯−1),cexp≤Mth​(0)≤Mth​(1)≤⋯≤Mth​(B¯−1).\begin{gathered}0\leq d_{t}^{h}(0)\leq d_{t}^{h}(1)\leq\cdots\leq d_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1),\\ c_{\mathrm{exp}}\leq M_{t}^{h}(0)\leq M_{t}^{h}(1)\leq\cdots\leq M_{t}^{h}(\bar{B}-1).\end{gathered}

Fix tt and self-confidence level jj, and define

τt,jqueue​(h):=min⁡({b∈{0,…,B¯−1}:Lh​(j)≤Mth​(b)}∪{B¯}).\tau_{t,j}^{\rm queue}(h):=\min\left(\left\{b\in\{0,\ldots,\bar{B}-1\}:L^{h}(j)\leq M_{t}^{h}(b)\right\}\cup\{\bar{B}\}\right).

By equation 4, the optimal policy with ties resolved in favor of acceptance therefore defers if and only if Bt<τt,jqueue​(h)B_{t}<\tau_{t,j}^{\rm queue}(h). ∎

Appendix B Proofs for Section 4.2

B.1 Proof sketch

To ease navigation within this appendix, we first provide a high-level proof sketch of our gap-dependent and worst-case upper bounds. They are proven in Appendices B.4 and  B.3 respectively.

Proof sketch. The analysis exploits that pessimism makes KL-PBD almost one-sided. On the high-probability event h¯t≤h⋆\underline{h}_{t}\leq h^{\star}, if the marginal cost of deferral were computed under the true model h⋆h^{\star}, the learner would accept only if the oracle does, and regret would come from deferrals only. This ordering is not exact, because h¯t\underline{h}_{t} is also plugged into the marginal cost of deferral. To account for these additional errors, we track the difference between the value functions of the pessimistic and true models: Proposition 2 relates this misspecification to the estimation error. Updating h¯t\underline{h}_{t} leaves an additional term controlled by its total variation, which is logarithmic. The remaining estimation error is charged only on deferred rounds, which are exactly the rounds that produce labels, so the confidence widths shrink as they are charged. Summing these widths incurs only an additive B¯\bar{B} per level from delayed feedback, since at most B¯\bar{B} previously deferred queries can still be unlabeled, and yields Theorem 2. For Theorem 1, we exploit that, by Proposition 2(ii), estimation errors smaller than γT/2\gamma_{T}/2 cannot change strict oracle decisions. We therefore compare h¯t\underline{h}_{t} with the intermediate model obtained by replacing h¯j,t\underline{h}_{j,t} with max⁡{h¯j,t,hj⋆−γT/2}\max\{\underline{h}_{j,t},h_{j}^{\star}-\gamma_{T}/2\}, which agrees with the oracle on every strict comparison. Only the confidence width beyond γT/2\gamma_{T}/2 needs to be charged, yielding the 1/γT1/\gamma_{T} dependence. ∎

+B¯​ce​(1+𝔼⁡[∑t=2σ−1(‖h¯t−h¯t−1‖∞+‖ht∘−ht−1∘‖∞)]).\displaystyle+\bar{B}c_{e}\left(1+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=2}^{\sigma-1}\left(\|\underline{h}_{t}-\underline{h}_{t-1}\|_{\infty}+\|h_{t}^{\circ}-h_{t-1}^{\circ}\|_{\infty}\right)\right]\right).

Proof of Theorem 1.

If 𝒢T=∅\mathcal{G}_{T}=\emptyset, the refined theorem gives zero regret. Otherwise, we apply Theorem 6 with aT=γT/2a_{T}=\gamma_{T}/2. We have (hj⋆−aT)+≤1(h_{j}^{\star}-a_{T})_{+}\leq 1 and, by Lemma 11, Ihj⋆​(aT)≤2/aT=4/γTI_{h_{j}^{\star}}(a_{T})\leq 2/a_{T}=4/\gamma_{T}. For ϕ⁡(T)=log⁡T+log⁡log⁡T\phi(T)=\log T+\log\log T, Lemma 8 gives ηT≤4​e​K​ϕ​(T)\eta_{T}\leq 4eK\phi(T). Consequently,

RT​(πKL-PBD)≤\displaystyle R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})\leq{} 4​e​K​ϕ​(T)​Δ+2​ce​∑j=1Kmin⁡{ωj​T,B¯+4​ϕ​(T)γT}\displaystyle 4eK\phi(T)\Delta+2c_{e}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\min\left\{\omega_{j}T,\,\bar{B}+\frac{4\phi(T)}{\gamma_{T}}\right\}
+2​B¯​ce​[1+4​∑j=1Klog⁡(1+ωj​Tϕ⁡(T))],\displaystyle+2\bar{B}c_{e}\left[1+4\sum_{j=1}^{K}\log\left(1+\frac{\omega_{j}T}{\phi(T)}\right)\right],

which proves the main-text theorem since κ=4​e​Δ\kappa=4e\Delta. ∎

In particular, the main-text bound implies

RT​(πKL-PBD)≤2​B¯​ce​(K+1)+K​ϕ​(T)​(8​ceγT+4​e​Δ)+8​B¯​ce​ΛT.R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})\leq 2\bar{B}c_{e}(K+1)+K\phi(T)\left(\frac{8c_{e}}{\gamma_{T}}+4e\Delta\right)+8\bar{B}c_{e}\Lambda_{T}.

When the gap is bounded away from zero, the regret remains logarithmic in TT. The failure contribution now has the same logarithmic order, but does not worsen the inverse-gap dependence. The refined theorem and equation 35 retain the variance-sensitive improvement.

B.5 Technical lemmas

B.5.1 Concentration and KL confidence bounds

Lemma 8 (Concentration within each self-confidence level under delayed feedback).

For every j∈[K]j\in[K], the observed-label sequence can be extended to an infinite i.i.d. Bernoulli⁡(hj⋆)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(h_{j}^{\star}) sequence. For any fixed budget ϕ⁡(T)>1\phi(T)>1, the event ℰ\mathcal{E} of equation 12 satisfies ℙ⁡(ℰc)≤ηT/T\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq\eta_{T}/T. For T≥3T\geq 3 and ϕ⁡(T)=log⁡T+log⁡log⁡T\phi(T)=\log T+\log\log T, we also have

ηT≤4​e​K​ϕ​(T).\eta_{T}\leq 4eK\phi(T). (26)
Proof.

Conditional on the self-confidence level sequence, the ground-truth labels are independent, with Yt∼Bernoulli⁡(hj⋆)Y_{t}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(h_{j}^{\star}) when Jt=jJ_{t}=j. Since deferral and completion decisions use only self-confidence levels, service information and previously revealed labels, conditional on the history immediately before a level-jj label is revealed, that label has distribution Bernoulli⁡(hj⋆)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(h_{j}^{\star}). Revealing completed labels in submission order within each round, and appending independent Bernoulli⁡(hj⋆)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(h_{j}^{\star}) labels after the observed sequence for level jj, gives the claimed infinite i.i.d. sequence (Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020, Section 4.6).

For a Bernoulli sample mean, Chernoff’s inequality and a union bound give

ℙ⁡(ℰc)≤2​K​T​e−ϕ⁡(T).\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq 2KTe^{-\phi(T)}.

For T≥2T\geq 2, applying the Bernoulli maximal inequality (Garivier, 2013, equation (5)) to the ground-truth label sequence for each self-confidence level and taking a union bound over levels gives

ℙ⁡(ℰc)≤2​e​K​⌈ϕ⁡(T)​log⁡T⌉​e−ϕ⁡(T),ϕ⁡(T)>1.\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq 2eK\lceil\phi(T)\log T\rceil e^{-\phi(T)},\qquad\phi(T)>1. (27)

If hj⋆∈{0,1}h_{j}^{\star}\in\{0,1\}, then h^j,n=hj⋆\widehat{h}_{j,n}=h_{j}^{\star} almost surely for every n≥1n\geq 1, so the KL concentration event holds automatically for that jj.

Combining these bounds with ℙ⁡(ℰc)≤1\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq 1 gives ℙ⁡(ℰc)≤ηT/T\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq\eta_{T}/T for T≥2T\geq 2. For T=1T=1, the same conclusion follows from the Chernoff union bound and the definition of η1\eta_{1}. Picking ϕ⁡(T)=log⁡T+log⁡log⁡T\phi(T)=\log{T}+\log\log{T} gives, using T​e−ϕ⁡(T)=(log⁡T)−1Te^{-\phi(T)}=(\log{T})^{-1},

ηT≤2​e​K​⌈ϕ⁡(T)​log⁡T⌉log⁡T≤2​e​K​(ϕ⁡(T)+1log⁡T)≤4​e​K​ϕ​(T).\eta_{T}\leq 2eK\frac{\lceil\phi(T)\log{T}\rceil}{\log{T}}\leq 2eK\left(\phi(T)+\frac{1}{\log{T}}\right)\leq 4eK\phi(T).

The last inequality uses log⁡T>1\log{T}>1 and ϕ⁡(T)>1\phi(T)>1. ∎

Lemma 9 (KL diameter and its integral bounds).

For every p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] and x≥0x\geq 0,

wp​(x)≤min⁡{p,2​x}.w_{p}(x)\leq\min\{p,\sqrt{2x}\}. (28)

Whenever n​kl⁡(h^j,n,hj⋆)≤ϕ⁡(T)n\operatorname{kl}(\widehat{h}_{j,n},h_{j}^{\star})\leq\phi(T) with n≥1n\geq 1,

0≤hj⋆−gj,n≤whj⋆​(ϕ⁡(T)/n).0\leq h_{j}^{\star}-g_{j,n}\leq w_{h_{j}^{\star}}(\phi(T)/n). (29)

Moreover, Fp,ΓF_{p,\Gamma} is nondecreasing and concave, and

Fp,Γ​(d)≤min⁡{p​d, 2​2​Γ​d}.F_{p,\Gamma}(d)\leq\min\left\{pd,\,2\sqrt{2\Gamma d}\right\}. (30)
Proof.

The full confidence set {q∈[0,1]:n​kl⁡(h^j,n,q)≤ϕ⁡(T)}\{q\in[0,1]:n\operatorname{kl}(\widehat{h}_{j,n},q)\leq\phi(T)\} is nonempty and compact. Its minimum is gj,ng_{j,n}, since it contains h^j,n\widehat{h}_{j,n}. Under the stated KL constraint, it also contains hj⋆h_{j}^{\star}. Thus gj,n≤hj⋆g_{j,n}\leq h_{j}^{\star}, and the definition of whj⋆w_{h_{j}^{\star}} gives equation 29.

The bound wp​(x)≤pw_{p}(x)\leq p is immediate. Pinsker’s inequality applied to each of the two KL constraints gives |z−p|,|z−q|≤x/2|z-p|,|z-q|\leq\sqrt{x/2}, hence p−q≤2​xp-q\leq\sqrt{2x}, proving equation 28.

As wpw_{p} is nondecreasing, the integrand defining Fp,ΓF_{p,\Gamma} is nonincreasing in uu, so Fp,ΓF_{p,\Gamma} is nondecreasing and concave. Integrating the two bounds in equation 28 gives equation 30. ∎

Lemma 10 (Pathwise total variation).

For any binary sequence and any fixed Γ>0\Gamma>0, let g0=0g_{0}=0 and let gng_{n} be its Bernoulli KL lower confidence bound with budget Γ\Gamma. For every integer N≥1N\geq 1,

∑n=1N|gn−gn−1|≤−2log(1−e−Γ/N)≤2log(1+N/Γ).\sum_{n=1}^{N}|g_{n}-g_{n-1}|\leq-2\log(1-e^{-\Gamma/N})\leq 2\log(1+N/\Gamma). (31)

For KL-PBD, on every sample path,

∑t=2T‖h¯t−h¯t−1‖∞≤2​∑j=1Klog⁡(1+Nj,Tϕ⁡(T)).\sum_{t=2}^{T}\|\underline{h}_{t}-\underline{h}_{t-1}\|_{\infty}\leq 2\sum_{j=1}^{K}\log\left(1+\frac{N_{j,T}}{\phi(T)}\right). (32)

Consequently,

𝔼⁡[∑t=2T‖h¯t−h¯t−1‖∞]≤2​ΛT.\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=2}^{T}\|\underline{h}_{t}-\underline{h}_{t-1}\|_{\infty}\right]\leq 2\Lambda_{T}. (33)
Proof.

We interpolate the number of successes ss and failures ff continuously. For s>0s>0, put m=s+fm=s+f, z=s/mz=s/m, and let q=q⁡(s,f)∈(0,z)q=q(s,f)\in(0,z) solve

m​kl⁡(z,q)=Γ.m\operatorname{kl}(z,q)=\Gamma.

For s=0s=0, set q⁡(0,f)=0q(0,f)=0, and set q⁡(0,0)=0q(0,0)=0. These definitions agree continuously at the boundaries relevant below: q≤zq\leq z gives continuity as s↓0s\downarrow 0 with f>0f>0, while kl⁡(z,q)≤kl⁡(1,q)=−log⁡q\operatorname{kl}(z,q)\leq\operatorname{kl}(1,q)=-\log q gives q≤e−Γ/mq\leq e^{-\Gamma/m} as m↓0m\downarrow 0. In particular, q(s,0)=e−Γ/sq(s,0)=e^{-\Gamma/s} for s>0s>0.

Consider first adding a success, keeping ff fixed. In the interior, implicit differentiation gives

∂∂s​[m​kl⁡(z,q)]q​ fixed=log⁡(z/q),∂∂q​[m​kl⁡(z,q)]=−m⁡(z−q)q⁡(1−q).\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\big[m\operatorname{kl}(z,q)\big]_{q\text{ fixed}}=\log(z/q),\qquad\frac{\partial}{\partial q}\big[m\operatorname{kl}(z,q)\big]=-\frac{m(z-q)}{q(1-q)}.

Writing a=log⁡(z/q)>0a=\log(z/q)>0 and x=Γ/mx=\Gamma/m, we obtain

∂q∂s=1−qm​aea−1≤Γm2​(eΓ/m−1).\frac{\partial q}{\partial s}=\frac{1-q}{m}\frac{a}{e^{a}-1}\leq\frac{\Gamma}{m^{2}(e^{\Gamma/m}-1)}. (34)

Indeed, x=z​a+(1−z)​log⁡((1−z)/(1−q))≤ax=za+(1-z)\log((1-z)/(1-q))\leq a, and a↦a/(ea−1)a\mapsto a/(e^{a}-1) is decreasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty). The same inequality holds when f=0f=0, either directly from q(s,0)=e−Γ/sq(s,0)=e^{-\Gamma/s} or by a limit.

Adding a failure while keeping ss fixed gives instead the partial derivative log⁡((1−z)/(1−q))≤0\log((1-z)/(1-q))\leq 0 at fixed qq. Implicit differentiation therefore gives ∂q/∂f≤0\partial q/\partial f\leq 0. Continuity extends this monotonicity to f=0f=0 and s=0s=0. Thus successes can only increase the lower confidence bound, and failures can only decrease it.

We interpolate each observation over its own interval m∈[n−1,n]m\in[n-1,n]. The total upward variation is at most the integral of the right-hand side of equation 34 over all intervals:

∑n=1N(gn−gn−1)+≤∫0NΓm2​(eΓ/m−1)dm=−log(1−e−Γ/N).\sum_{n=1}^{N}(g_{n}-g_{n-1})_{+}\leq\int_{0}^{N}\frac{\Gamma}{m^{2}(e^{\Gamma/m}-1)}\,dm=-\log(1-e^{-\Gamma/N}).

By continuity of the lower confidence bound at m=0m=0 and s=0s=0, the integrals may start at 00. Since g0=0g_{0}=0 and gN≥0g_{N}\geq 0, downward variation is no larger than upward variation. Finally, ex≥1+xe^{x}\geq 1+x implies −log⁡(1−e−x)≤log⁡(1+1/x)-\log(1-e^{-x})\leq\log(1+1/x), proving equation 31.

Fix a self-confidence level jj. Since Nj,tN_{j,t} is nondecreasing and h¯j,t=gj,Nj,t\underline{h}_{j,t}=g_{j,N_{j,t}}, the triangle inequality gives

∑t=2T|h¯j,t−h¯j,t−1|≤∑n=1Nj,T|gj,n−gj,n−1|.\sum_{t=2}^{T}\left|\underline{h}_{j,t}-\underline{h}_{j,t-1}\right|\leq\sum_{n=1}^{N_{j,T}}|g_{j,n}-g_{j,n-1}|.

Applying equation 31, with an empty sum when Nj,T=0N_{j,T}=0, and using

‖h¯t−h¯t−1‖∞≤∑j=1K|h¯j,t−h¯j,t−1|\left\|\underline{h}_{t}-\underline{h}_{t-1}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{K}\left|\underline{h}_{j,t}-\underline{h}_{j,t-1}\right|

proves equation 32.

It remains to take expectations. Since Nj,TN_{j,T} counts completed self-confidence level jj labels available before round TT, it is bounded by the number of self-confidence level jj arrivals before that round. Thus 𝔼⁡[Nj,T]≤ωj​T\mathbb{E}[N_{j,T}]\leq\omega_{j}T. By concavity of x↦log⁡(1+x)x\mapsto\log(1+x),

𝔼⁡[∑t=2T‖h¯t−h¯t−1‖∞]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=2}^{T}\left\|\underline{h}_{t}-\underline{h}_{t-1}\right\|_{\infty}\right] ≤2​∑j=1K𝔼⁡[log⁡(1+Nj,Tϕ⁡(T))]\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\left(1+\frac{N_{j,T}}{\phi(T)}\right)\right]
≤2​∑j=1Klog⁡(1+ωj​Tϕ⁡(T))=2​ΛT.\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{j=1}^{K}\log\left(1+\frac{\omega_{j}T}{\phi(T)}\right)=2\Lambda_{T}.

∎

Lemma 11 (Integrated residual width).

If p≤ap\leq a, then Ip​(a)=0I_{p}(a)=0. For p>a>0p>a>0,

Ip​(a)≤min⁡{2a, 8​p​(1−p)​(1a−1p)+12​log⁡pa}.I_{p}(a)\leq\min\left\{\frac{2}{a},\,8p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{p}\right)+12\log\frac{p}{a}\right\}. (35)
Proof.

For p≤ap\leq a, Ip​(a)=0I_{p}(a)=0. Pinsker’s bound gives, for a>0a>0,

Ip​(a)≤∫0∞(2/u−a)+​𝑑u=2a.I_{p}(a)\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}(\sqrt{2/u}-a)_{+}\,du=\frac{2}{a}.

For the other bound, assume p>ap>a and put A=2​2​p​(1−p)A=2\sqrt{2p(1-p)}. By Tonelli’s theorem,

Ip​(a)=∫apLeb⁡{u>0:wp​(1/u)>r}​𝑑r.I_{p}(a)=\int_{a}^{p}\operatorname{Leb}\{u>0:w_{p}(1/u)>r\}\,dr. (36)

If wp​(1/u)>rw_{p}(1/u)>r, then equation 28 gives r<A/u+6/ur<A/\sqrt{u}+6/u. By 2​x​y≤x2+y22xy\leq x^{2}+y^{2}, applied with x=rx=\sqrt{r} and y=A/r​uy=A/\sqrt{ru},

Au≤r2+A22​r​u.\frac{A}{\sqrt{u}}\leq\frac{r}{2}+\frac{A^{2}}{2ru}.

Consequently,

r<r2+A22​r​u+6u,sou<A2r2+12r.r<\frac{r}{2}+\frac{A^{2}}{2ru}+\frac{6}{u},\qquad\text{so}\qquad u<\frac{A^{2}}{r^{2}}+\frac{12}{r}.

Thus

Leb⁡{u>0:wp​(1/u)>r}≤A2r2+12r.\operatorname{Leb}\{u>0:w_{p}(1/u)>r\}\leq\frac{A^{2}}{r^{2}}+\frac{12}{r}.

This argument also applies when A=0A=0. Substituting this length bound into equation 36 yields

Ip​(a)≤8​p​(1−p)​(1a−1p)+12​log⁡pa,I_{p}(a)\leq 8p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{p}\right)+12\log\frac{p}{a},

as claimed. In particular, all integrals used in the theorems are finite. ∎

B.5.2 Service-capacity stability bounds

Recall from Appendix A the queue value Uth​(b):=∑j=0Kωj​Vth​((b,j)).U_{t}^{h}(b):=\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}V_{t}^{h}((b,j)). Since VT+1h​((b,j))=D⁡(b)V_{T+1}^{h}((b,j))=D(b) for every j=0,…,Kj=0,\ldots,K and ∑j=0Kωj=1\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}=1, we have UT+1h=DU_{T+1}^{h}=D, independently of hh, and the Bellman recursion can be written as

Uth​(b)=chold​b+∑j=0Kωj​mina∈𝒜⁡(b,j)​{cexp​a+Lh​(j)​(1−a)+𝔼⁡[Ut+1h​((b+a−Ct)+)]}.U_{t}^{h}(b)=c_{\mathrm{hold}}b+\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}\min_{a\in\mathcal{A}(b,j)}\left\{c_{\mathrm{exp}}a+L^{h}(j)(1-a)+\mathbb{E}\!\left[U_{t+1}^{h}((b+a-C_{t})^{+})\right]\right\}.

We first show that the service-capacity structure yields a stability property useful to control the effect of a pessimistic conditional accuracy vector on the Bellman recursion.

Proposition 2 (Bellman stability).

Let h,h~∈[0,1]Kh,\widetilde{h}\in[0,1]^{K}. For every t≤Tt\leq T:

  1. (i)

    0≤Mth​(b)−Mth~​(b)≤ce​‖h−h~‖∞.0\leq M_{t}^{h}(b)-M_{t}^{\widetilde{h}}(b)\leq c_{e}\|h-\widetilde{h}\|_{\infty}.

Part (i) controls changes in the Bellman quantities under arbitrary conditional accuracy perturbations, while part (ii) shows that a pessimistic conditional accuracy vector increases the Bellman marginal deferral costs and induces an ordered change in the queue values.

Proof of Proposition 2.

Let h,h~∈[0,1]Kh,\widetilde{h}\in[0,1]^{K} and set ε:=ce​‖h−h~‖∞\varepsilon:=c_{e}\|h-\widetilde{h}\|_{\infty}. |xth​(q)−xth~​(q)|≤ε,\left|x_{t}^{h}(q)-x_{t}^{\widetilde{h}}(q)\right|\leq\varepsilon, (37)

At t=T+1t=T+1, both queue-value functions are equal. Hence xT+1h​(q)=xT+1h~​(q)x_{T+1}^{h}(q)=x_{T+1}^{\widetilde{h}}(q) for every q=1,…,B¯q=1,\ldots,\bar{B}, so both claims hold. Suppose they hold at time t+1t+1. By equation 7, for every b<B¯b<\bar{B},

The weights are nonnegative and sum to at most one. Therefore,

|dth​(b)−dth~​(b)|≤ε,\left|d_{t}^{h}(b)-d_{t}^{\widetilde{h}}(b)\right|\leq\varepsilon,

We next record a uniform bound on the gaps Δt\Delta_{t}.

Lemma 12 (Uniform gap bound).

For every conditional accuracy vector hh, every t≤T+1t\leq T+1, and every q=1,…,B¯q=1,\ldots,\bar{B},

0≤Uth​(q)−Uth​(q−1)≤q​choldμ+(ce−cexp)+.0\leq U_{t}^{h}(q)-U_{t}^{h}(q-1)\leq\frac{q\,c_{\mathrm{hold}}}{\mu}+(c_{e}-c_{\mathrm{exp}})_{+}. (39)

cexp≤Mth​(b)≤max⁡{ce,cexp}+chold​B¯μ.c_{\mathrm{exp}}\leq M_{t}^{h}(b)\leq\max\{c_{e},c_{\mathrm{exp}}\}+\frac{c_{\mathrm{hold}}\bar{B}}{\mu}. (40)

In particular, 0≤Δt≤Δ0\leq\Delta_{t}\leq\Delta on every sample path.

Proof.

The lower bound in equation 39 follows from Lemma 3. For the upper bound, fix tt and q≥1q\geq 1, and couple two systems starting from queue states qq and q−1q-1, respectively, using the same self-confidence level and service realizations through round TT, and the same service realizations thereafter. Let the lower system follow an optimal policy.

To account for the terminal value, we regard both systems as continuing after round TT with no further arrivals and incurring holding costs until their queues are empty; by definition, the expected cost of this continuation from queue state bb is D⁡(b)D(b).

While the queues differ, they differ by exactly one job. If the lower system takes action 00, let the upper system also take action 00. If the lower system defers, let the upper system take action 00 instead. In the latter case, the two pre-service queue states after the deferral decision coincide, and hence the queues couple at the end of that round. Once they have coupled, let the upper system follow the same actions as the lower system.

Before coupling, the difference in holding cost is choldc_{\mathrm{hold}} per round. If the lower system never triggers coupling by deferring, the queues couple once qq rounds with Ct≥1C_{t}\geq 1 have occurred. The expected time required for qq such service opportunities is q/μq/\mu. If coupling instead occurs because the lower system defers, the only additional non-holding cost incurred by the upper system on that round is ce​(1−hJt)−cexp≤(ce−cexp)+.c_{e}(1-h_{J_{t}})-c_{\mathrm{exp}}\leq(c_{e}-c_{\mathrm{exp}})_{+}. This can occur at most once. Thus the constructed algorithm for the upper system has expected cost at most

Uth​(q−1)+q​choldμ+(ce−cexp)+.U_{t}^{h}(q-1)+\frac{q\,c_{\mathrm{hold}}}{\mu}+(c_{e}-c_{\mathrm{exp}})_{+}.

Optimality of Uth​(q)U_{t}^{h}(q) proves equation 39.

By equation 7,

dth​(b)=∑c=0bρC​(c)​xt+1h​(b+1−c).d_{t}^{h}(b)=\sum_{c=0}^{b}\rho_{C}(c)\,x_{t+1}^{h}(b+1-c).

Using equation 39 and b+1≤B¯b+1\leq\bar{B},

0≤dth​(b)≤chold​B¯μ+(ce−cexp)+.0\leq d_{t}^{h}(b)\leq\frac{c_{\mathrm{hold}}\bar{B}}{\mu}+(c_{e}-c_{\mathrm{exp}})_{+}.

Together with equation 6, this yields equation 40.

Finally, for j∈[K]j\in[K], ce​(1−hj⋆)∈[0,ce]c_{e}(1-h_{j}^{\star})\in[0,c_{e}], while equation 40 gives 0≤Mt⋆​(b)≤Δ0\leq M_{t}^{\star}(b)\leq\Delta. Hence, for b<B¯b<\bar{B},

|ce​(1−hj⋆)−Mt⋆​(b)|≤Δ.\left|c_{e}(1-h_{j}^{\star})-M_{t}^{\star}(b)\right|\leq\Delta.

On no-query or full-queue rounds Δt=0\Delta_{t}=0. Thus the definition of Δt\Delta_{t} gives 0≤Δt≤Δ0\leq\Delta_{t}\leq\Delta on every sample path.

∎

Lemma 14 (Pending-label bound for deferred queries).

For j∈[K]j\in[K] and any nonnegative nonincreasing function f:[0,∞)→[0,∞)f:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty),

𝔼⁡[∑t<σ𝟏​{Jt=j,At=1}​f​(Nj,t)]≤min⁡{f⁡(0)​ωj​T,B¯​f​(0)+∫0ωj​Tf⁡(u)​𝑑u}.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t<\sigma}\mathbf{1}\{J_{t}=j,A_{t}=1\}f(N_{j,t})\right]\leq\min\left\{f(0)\omega_{j}T,\ \bar{B}f(0)+\int_{0}^{\omega_{j}T}f(u)\,du\right\}.

Fix a self-confidence level jj, write Dj:=Dj,σ−1D_{j}:=D_{j,\sigma-1}, and enumerate its deferrals before σ\sigma as tj,1,…,tj,Djt_{j,1},\ldots,t_{j,D_{j}}. Since deferral is feasible at tj,ℓt_{j,\ell}, at most B¯−1\bar{B}-1 of them can still be pending. Hence

Nj,tj,ℓ≥(ℓ−B¯)+.N_{j,t_{j,\ell}}\geq(\ell-\bar{B})_{+}. (45)

∑ℓ=1Djf⁡(Nj,tj,ℓ)≤f⁡(0)​min⁡{Dj,B¯}+∑n=1(Dj−B¯)+f⁡(n).\sum_{\ell=1}^{D_{j}}f(N_{j,t_{j,\ell}})\leq f(0)\min\{D_{j},\bar{B}\}+\sum_{n=1}^{(D_{j}-\bar{B})_{+}}f(n).

Since ff is nonincreasing, f⁡(n)≤∫n−1nf⁡(u)​𝑑uf(n)\leq\int_{n-1}^{n}f(u)\,du. Thus

∑ℓ=1Djf⁡(Nj,tj,ℓ)\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{D_{j}}f(N_{j,t_{j,\ell}}) ≤f⁡(0)​min⁡{Dj,B¯}+∫0(Dj−B¯)+f⁡(u)​𝑑u\displaystyle\leq f(0)\min\{D_{j},\bar{B}\}+\int_{0}^{(D_{j}-\bar{B})_{+}}f(u)\,du
≤B¯​f​(0)+∫0Djf⁡(u)​du.\displaystyle\leq\bar{B}f(0)+\int_{0}^{D_{j}}f(u)\,du.

Every such deferral occurs on a self-confidence level jj arrival, so 𝔼⁡[Dj]≤ωj​T\mathbb{E}[D_{j}]\leq\omega_{j}T. The map d↦∫0df⁡(u)​𝑑ud\mapsto\int_{0}^{d}f(u)\,du is nondecreasing and concave because ff is nonnegative and nonincreasing. Consequently, Jensen’s inequality gives

𝔼⁡[∑ℓ=1Djf⁡(Nj,tj,ℓ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{D_{j}}f(N_{j,t_{j,\ell}})\right] ≤B¯​f​(0)+𝔼⁡[∫0Djf⁡(u)​du]\displaystyle\leq\bar{B}f(0)+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{D_{j}}f(u)\,du\right]
≤B¯​f​(0)+∫0𝔼⁡[Dj]f⁡(u)​𝑑u\displaystyle\leq\bar{B}f(0)+\int_{0}^{\mathbb{E}[D_{j}]}f(u)\,du
≤B¯​f​(0)+∫0ωj​Tf⁡(u)​du.\displaystyle\leq\bar{B}f(0)+\int_{0}^{\omega_{j}T}f(u)\,du.

On the other hand, f⁡(Nj,t)≤f⁡(0)f(N_{j,t})\leq f(0) gives

B.6 Extension to unknown arrival and service distributions

The arrival distribution ω\omega and the truncated service distribution defined below can be learned without additional deferrals when their realizations are observed independently of the deferral decisions. In this section, we show that using KL-PBD with plug-in empirical estimates of these distributions preserves the worst-case regret rate of Theorem 2, including its dependence on the arrival distribution ω\omega. Throughout this section, assume chold>0c_{\mathrm{hold}}>0. For unknown ρC\rho_{C}, additionally assume that C¯t:=min⁡{Ct,B¯}\bar{C}_{t}:=\min\{C_{t},\bar{B}\} is observed at the end of every round, including rounds with an empty queue. Theorem 7 shows that learning these distributions requires no additional exploration under the stated observation assumptions and does not worsen the worst-case rate of Theorem 2.

Appendix C Proofs for Section 5

C.1 Proof sketches

To ease navigation within this appendix, we first provide high-level proof sketches of our instance-dependent and minimax lower bounds. They are proven in Appendices C.3 and  C.5 respectively.

Proof sketch of Theorem 3. We first reduce to the long-horizon problem, in which the oracle threshold no longer depends on the round; passing from long-horizon to finite-horizon regret costs only an O⁡(1)O(1) additive term (Lemma 16). For a fixed level jj with hj⋆>τ¯⋆h_{j}^{\star}>\overline{\tau}^{\star}, the long-horizon optimal policy accepts level jj at every queue state, whereas deferring incurs an extra cost of at least ce​(hj⋆−τ¯⋆)c_{e}(h_{j}^{\star}-\overline{\tau}^{\star}). We compare h⋆h^{\star} with an alternative instance in which only hj⋆h_{j}^{\star} is moved slightly below τ¯⋆\overline{\tau}^{\star}. Although the deferral threshold changes with the instance, we show that deferring level jj is strictly beneficial in the long run under the alternative (equation 78), so a uniformly efficient learner must behave differently on the two instances. Since only completed level-jj reviews distinguish them (Lemma 17), a change-of-measure argument (Lai and Robbins, 1985) forces order log⁡T/kl⁡(hj⋆,τ¯⋆)\log T/\operatorname{kl}(h_{j}^{\star},\overline{\tau}^{\star}) level-jj deferrals under h⋆h^{\star}. Multiplying by their extra cost ce​(hj⋆−τ¯⋆)c_{e}(h_{j}^{\star}-\overline{\tau}^{\star}) yields the corresponding term in Theorem 3. Levels with hj⋆<τ¯⋆h_{j}^{\star}<\overline{\tau}^{\star} are instead always deferred by the oracle at the empty queue, so they can be reviewed without taking a suboptimal action. ∎

Proof sketch of Theorem 4. When μ=1\mu=1, we move each conditional accuracy hjh_{j} a distance δj\delta_{j} above or below the oracle’s accuracy threshold, so that two neighboring instances differing only at level jj have different optimal actions for level-jj queries. With δj≍min{1,(ωjT)−1/2}\delta_{j}\asymp\min\{1,(\omega_{j}T)^{-1/2}\}, Lemma 17 implies that the corresponding histories remain statistically indistinguishable, so on one of the two instances the learner must take the suboptimal action on a constant fraction of these queries, each costing order ce​δjc_{e}\delta_{j}. When μ<1\mu<1, perturbing the accuracies moves the threshold they are compared with. We therefore shift all coordinates of each perturbed instance by a common amount until the long-horizon empty-queue threshold coincides with the center of the perturbation (Lemma 21). An additional difficulty is that the two neighboring instances are only guaranteed to have different optimal actions when the queue is empty; by keeping the queue occupied, the learner could reduce the number of rounds on which indistinguishability translates into regret. Lemmas 20 and 22 show that this is not free: if the queue is rarely empty, the learner must defer sufficiently often while it is congested, at a cost of order choldc_{\rm hold}. Capping δj\delta_{j} at the holding-cost scale keeps this cost uniformly positive and produces the second term in the minimum, yielding Theorem 4. ∎

C.3 Instance-dependent regret lower bound

We show that every uniformly efficient algorithm must collect order log⁡T\log T expert labels at each self-confidence level where the oracle accepts, by comparing the true instance with an alternative on which deferral is strictly beneficial.

Proof.

Let u⋆:=uh⋆u^{\star}:=u_{h^{\star}} be the bias from Lemma 16, set 𝔡⋆:=𝔡h⋆\mathfrak{d}_{\star}:=\mathfrak{d}_{h^{\star}}, so that M¯⋆​(0)=cexp+(P1−P0)​u⋆​(0)\overline{M}^{\star}(0)=c_{\rm exp}+(P_{1}-P_{0})u^{\star}(0) and τ¯⋆=1−M¯⋆​(0)/ce\overline{\tau}^{\star}=1-\overline{M}^{\star}(0)/c_{e} by Lemma 18. Remark 2.

When μ=1\mu=1, τ¯⋆=1−cexp/ce\overline{\tau}^{\star}=1-c_{\rm exp}/c_{e}, and Theorem 3 can alternatively be derived from the Graves–Lai lower bound for structured MDPs (Ok et al., 2018, Theorem 1).

C.4 KL-PBD is asymptotically optimal under immediate-service

In this section, we show that KL-PBD matches Theorem 3 when service is immediate (μ=1)(\mu=1).

Throughout this subsection, Ct≥1C_{t}\geq 1 almost surely and 0<cexp<ce0<c_{\rm exp}<c_{e}. Thus μ=1\mu=1 and τ=1−cexp/ce∈(0,1)\tau=1-c_{\rm exp}/c_{e}\in(0,1). We consider KL-PBD with a fixed budget ϕ⁡(T)>0\phi(T)>0. All probabilities and expectations in this subsection are under h⋆h^{\star} and πKL-PBD\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}}.

By equation 75 with μ=1\mu=1, Mth​(0)=cexpM_{t}^{h}(0)=c_{\mathrm{exp}} for every hh and tt. Thus, after nn completed level jj reviews, the algorithm defers exactly when gj,n<τg_{j,n}<\tau, with ties resolved in favor of acceptance.

Every deferral yields a label before the next round. The sample counts before successive level jj deferrals are therefore 0,1,…,Dj,T−10,1,\ldots,D_{j,T}-1. We use the infinite i.i.d. ground-truth label sequences for each self-confidence level from Lemma 8.

Lemma 19 (Erroneous acceptance under immediate service).

For a level jj with 0<hj⋆<τ0<h_{j}^{\star}<\tau,

𝔼⁡[∑t=1T𝟏​{Jt=j,At=0}]≤T​e−ϕ⁡(T)exp⁡{kl⁡(τ,hj⋆)}−1.\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{1}\{J_{t}=j,A_{t}=0\}\right]\leq\frac{Te^{-\phi(T)}}{\exp\{\operatorname{kl}(\tau,h_{j}^{\star})\}-1}. (83)

If hj⋆=0h_{j}^{\star}=0, the left-hand side is zero.

Proof.

Fix jj with 0<hj⋆<τ0<h_{j}^{\star}<\tau. The algorithm accepts only when gj,n≥τg_{j,n}\geq\tau and hence n≥1n\geq 1, since gj,0=0g_{j,0}=0. For every z∈[τ,1]z\in[\tau,1],

≥kl⁡(τ,hj⋆).\displaystyle\geq\operatorname{kl}(\tau,h_{j}^{\star}).

ℙ⁡(gj,n≥τ)≤ℙ⁡(h^j,n≥zn)≤e−n​kl⁡(zn,hj⋆)≤e−ϕ⁡(T)−n​kl⁡(τ,hj⋆).\mathbb{P}(g_{j,n}\geq\tau)\leq\mathbb{P}(\widehat{h}_{j,n}\geq z_{n})\leq e^{-n\operatorname{kl}(z_{n},h_{j}^{\star})}\leq e^{-\phi(T)-n\operatorname{kl}(\tau,h_{j}^{\star})}.

ℙ(∃n≥1:gj,n≥τ)≤∑n=1∞e−ϕ⁡(T)−n​kl⁡(τ,hj⋆)=e−ϕ⁡(T)exp⁡{kl⁡(τ,hj⋆)}−1.\mathbb{P}(\exists n\geq 1:g_{j,n}\geq\tau)\leq\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}e^{-\phi(T)-n\operatorname{kl}(\tau,h_{j}^{\star})}=\frac{e^{-\phi(T)}}{\exp\{\operatorname{kl}(\tau,h_{j}^{\star})\}-1}.

Since

∑t=1T𝟏​{Jt=j,At=0}≤T​𝟏​{∃n≥1:gj,n≥τ},\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{1}\{J_{t}=j,A_{t}=0\}\leq T\mathbf{1}\{\exists n\geq 1:g_{j,n}\geq\tau\},

taking expectations proves the bound. If hj⋆=0h_{j}^{\star}=0, all sample means and lower confidence bounds are zero, so every level jj query is deferred. ∎

Proposition 3 (Asymptotic optimality under immediate service).

For fixed KK, any budget sequence satisfying ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→1\phi(T)/\log T\to 1 makes KL-PBD uniformly efficient on the immediate-service class. If, in addition, T​e−ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→0Te^{-\phi(T)}/\log T\to 0, then, for every fixed immediate-service instance,

limT→∞RT​(πKL-PBD)log⁡T=ce​∑j∈[K]hj⋆>τ,ωj>0hj⋆−τkl⁡(hj⋆,τ).\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})}{\log T}=c_{e}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in[K]\\ h_{j}^{\star}>\tau,\ \omega_{j}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{h_{j}^{\star}-\tau}{\operatorname{kl}(h_{j}^{\star},\tau)}.

In particular, the equality holds for ϕ⁡(T)=log⁡T+log⁡log⁡T\phi(T)=\log T+\log\log T and ϕ⁡(T)=log⁡T\phi(T)=\log T for T≥3T\geq 3, with arbitrary positive budgets for smaller horizons. If hj⋆≥τh_{j}^{\star}\geq\tau for every j∈[K]j\in[K] with ωj>0\omega_{j}>0, the condition T​e−ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→0Te^{-\phi(T)}/\log T\to 0 is unnecessary.

Proof.
