Dj,T≤⌈ϕ⁡(T)d⌉+∑n=1∞𝟏{h^j,n<hj⋆−ε}.D_{j,T}\leq\left\lceil\frac{\phi(T)}{d}\right\rceil+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{h}_{j,n}<h_{j}^{\star}-\varepsilon\}.

Taking expectations and applying the Bernoulli Chernoff bound gives

𝔼⁡[Dj,T]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[D_{j,T}] ≤⌈ϕ⁡(T)d⌉+∑n=1∞e−n​kl⁡(hj⋆−ε,hj⋆)\displaystyle\leq\left\lceil\frac{\phi(T)}{d}\right\rceil+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}e^{-n\operatorname{kl}(h_{j}^{\star}-\varepsilon,h_{j}^{\star})}
≤1+ϕ⁡(T)kl⁡(hj⋆−ε,τ)+1exp⁡{kl⁡(hj⋆−ε,hj⋆)}−1\displaystyle\leq 1+\frac{\phi(T)}{\operatorname{kl}(h_{j}^{\star}-\varepsilon,\tau)}+\frac{1}{\exp\{\operatorname{kl}(h_{j}^{\star}-\varepsilon,h_{j}^{\star})\}-1} (84)

where the final term is interpreted as zero when the divergence is infinite. In particular, this covers hj⋆=1h_{j}^{\star}=1.

We next prove uniform efficiency. By Lemma 2, under immediate service,

RT​(πKL-PBD)=\displaystyle R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})={} ce​∑j∈[K]hj⋆>τ,ωj>0(hj⋆−τ)​𝔼​[Dj,T]\displaystyle c_{e}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in[K]\\ h_{j}^{\star}>\tau,\ \omega_{j}>0\end{subarray}}(h_{j}^{\star}-\tau)\mathbb{E}[D_{j,T}]
+ce∑j∈[K]hj⋆​<τ,ωj>​0(τ−hj⋆)𝔼[∑t=1T𝟏{Jt=j,At=0}].\displaystyle+c_{e}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in[K]\\ h_{j}^{\star}<\tau,\ \omega_{j}>0\end{subarray}}(\tau-h_{j}^{\star})\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{1}\{J_{t}=j,A_{t}=0\}\right].

Levels jj with hj⋆=τh_{j}^{\star}=\tau or ωj=0\omega_{j}=0 contribute zero regret. If hj⋆=0h_{j}^{\star}=0, KL-PBD never accepts at level jj. By Lemma 19, the second term is at most

ce​T​e−ϕ⁡(T)​∑j∈[K]0<hj⋆​<τ,ωj>​0τ−hj⋆exp⁡{kl⁡(τ,hj⋆)}−1.c_{e}Te^{-\phi(T)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in[K]\\ 0<h_{j}^{\star}<\tau,\ \omega_{j}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{\tau-h_{j}^{\star}}{\exp\{\operatorname{kl}(\tau,h_{j}^{\star})\}-1}. (85)

If ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→1\phi(T)/\log T\to 1, then T​e−ϕ⁡(T)=exp⁡{o⁡(log⁡T)}=o⁡(Tα)Te^{-\phi(T)}=\exp\{o(\log T)\}=o(T^{\alpha}) for every α>0\alpha>0, while equation 84 gives 𝔼⁡[Dj,T]=O⁡(log⁡T)\mathbb{E}[D_{j,T}]=O(\log T) for every jj with hj⋆>τh_{j}^{\star}>\tau. Thus KL-PBD is uniformly efficient on the immediate-service class.

It remains to identify the asymptotic coefficient. Dividing equation 84 by log⁡T\log T, using ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→1\phi(T)/\log T\to 1, and then letting ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 gives, for every jj with hj⋆>τh_{j}^{\star}>\tau,

lim supT→∞𝔼⁡[Dj,T]log⁡T≤1kl⁡(hj⋆,τ).\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[D_{j,T}]}{\log T}\leq\frac{1}{\operatorname{kl}(h_{j}^{\star},\tau)}.

If, in addition, T​e−ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→0Te^{-\phi(T)}/\log T\to 0, then equation 85 is o⁡(log⁡T)o(\log T). Since KK is finite,

lim supT→∞RT​(πKL-PBD)log⁡T≤ce​∑j∈[K]hj⋆>τ,ωj>0hj⋆−τkl⁡(hj⋆,τ).\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{R_{T}(\pi^{\texttt{KL-PBD}})}{\log T}\leq c_{e}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in[K]\\ h_{j}^{\star}>\tau,\ \omega_{j}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{h_{j}^{\star}-\tau}{\operatorname{kl}(h_{j}^{\star},\tau)}.

Uniform efficiency and Theorem 3 give the matching lower bound, proving the claimed limit.

If hj⋆≥τh_{j}^{\star}\geq\tau for every j∈[K]j\in[K] with ωj>0\omega_{j}>0, the acceptance contribution is identically zero. Hence the same upper coefficient follows from equation 84 under ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→1\phi(T)/\log T\to 1 alone, and the lower bound again gives equality.

Finally, both ϕ⁡(T)=log⁡T+log⁡log⁡T\phi(T)=\log T+\log\log T and ϕ⁡(T)=log⁡T\phi(T)=\log T satisfy ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→1\phi(T)/\log T\to 1 and T​e−ϕ⁡(T)/log⁡T→0Te^{-\phi(T)}/\log T\to 0. ∎

Remark 3 (Worst case over ω\omega).

The function f⁡(x)=min⁡{x,x}f(x)=\min\{x,\sqrt{x}\} is nondecreasing and concave on [0,∞)[0,\infty), so Jensen’s inequality gives ∑j=1Kf⁡(ωj​T)≤K​f​(T/K)=min⁡{T,K​T}\sum_{j=1}^{K}f(\omega_{j}T)\leq Kf(T/K)=\min\{T,\sqrt{KT}\}, with equality when ω0=0\omega_{0}=0 and ωj=1/K\omega_{j}=1/K for every j∈[K]j\in[K].

C.6 Technical lemmas

C.6.1 Proofs of the common ingredients

Proof of Lemma 16.

By Lemma 3, each ξsh\xi_{s}^{h} is nonnegative and nondecreasing in qq. Its update is given by equation 7, equation 9, and equation 10.

Write gD​(q):=D⁡(q)−D⁡(q−1)g_{D}(q):=D(q)-D(q-1) and d0​(b):=∑c=0bρC​(c)​gD​(b+1−c)d_{0}(b):=\sum_{c=0}^{b}\rho_{C}(c)g_{D}(b+1-c). Differencing equation 63 gives gD​(q)=chold+d0​(q−1)g_{D}(q)=c_{\rm hold}+d_{0}(q-1). Since DD is discrete convex, d0d_{0} is nondecreasing. The median or maximum in the increment update is therefore at least d0​(q−1)d_{0}(q-1), giving ξ1h​(q)≥gD​(q)=ξ0h​(q)\xi_{1}^{h}(q)\geq g_{D}(q)=\xi_{0}^{h}(q). The update is coordinatewise nondecreasing, so ξs+1h≥ξsh\xi_{s+1}^{h}\geq\xi_{s}^{h} for every s≥0s\geq 0.

By equation 39, ξsh​(q)≤q​chold/μ+(ce−cexp)+\xi_{s}^{h}(q)\leq qc_{\rm hold}/\mu+(c_{e}-c_{\rm exp})_{+}, uniformly in ss. Hence ξsh​(q)↑xh​(q)\xi_{s}^{h}(q)\uparrow x_{h}(q), and Wsh​(b)−Wsh​(0)→uh​(b):=∑q=1bxh​(q)W_{s}^{h}(b)-W_{s}^{h}(0)\to u_{h}(b):=\sum_{q=1}^{b}x_{h}(q). In particular, uh≥Du_{h}\geq D because ξ0h=gD\xi_{0}^{h}=g_{D}.

Let 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h} be the queue Bellman operator. With vsh:=Wsh−Wsh​(0)v_{s}^{h}:=W_{s}^{h}-W_{s}^{h}(0) and gsh:=Ws+1h​(0)−Wsh​(0)g_{s}^{h}:=W_{s+1}^{h}(0)-W_{s}^{h}(0), translation invariance gives gsh+vs+1h=𝒯h​vshg_{s}^{h}+v_{s+1}^{h}=\mathcal{T}_{h}v_{s}^{h} and gsh=(𝒯h​vsh)​(0)g_{s}^{h}=(\mathcal{T}_{h}v_{s}^{h})(0). The operator is continuous because the state and action spaces are finite. Thus gsh→gh:=(𝒯h​uh)​(0)g_{s}^{h}\to g_{h}:=(\mathcal{T}_{h}u_{h})(0), and passing to the limit yields equation 64. Passing the increment identities to the limit proves (i) and preserves monotonicity and discrete convexity.

For (ii), equation 66 shows that dh​(b)d_{h}(b) is nonnegative and nondecreasing in bb. At the empty queue, dh​(0)=ρC​(0)​xh​(1)=(1−μ)​uh​(1)d_{h}(0)=\rho_{C}(0)x_{h}(1)=(1-\mu)u_{h}(1), proving equation 69.

For (iii), using equation 64, independence of JtJ_{t} from ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}, and the tower property,

𝔼hπ​[∑t=1Tℓh​(Bt,Jt,At)+D⁡(BT+1)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{h}^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{h}(B_{t},J_{t},A_{t})+D(B_{T+1})\right] =T​gh+𝔼⁡[uh​(B1)]+𝔼hπ​[(D−uh)​(BT+1)]\displaystyle={}Tg_{h}+\mathbb{E}[u_{h}(B_{1})]+\mathbb{E}_{h}^{\pi}[(D-u_{h})(B_{T+1})]
+𝔼hπ​[∑t=1T𝔡h​(Bt,Jt,At)].\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{h}^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathfrak{d}_{h}(B_{t},J_{t},A_{t})\right]. (100)

A stationary policy attaining the minima in equation 64 has zero disadvantage. Therefore every algorithm has cost at least T​gh+𝔼⁡[uh​(B1)]+minb⁡(D−uh)​(b)Tg_{h}+\mathbb{E}[u_{h}(B_{1})]+\min_{b}(D-u_{h})(b), while that stationary policy has cost at most the same expression with the minimum replaced by the maximum. The finite-horizon optimum lies between these two quantities, which proves equation 70.

For (iv), evaluating the minimum in equation 64 at the action distribution of φ\varphi gives gh+uh​(b)≤∑j=0Kωj​∑aφ⁡(a∣b,j)​{ℓh​(b,j,a)+(Pa​uh)​(b)}g_{h}+u_{h}(b)\leq\sum_{j=0}^{K}\omega_{j}\sum_{a}\varphi(a\mid b,j)\{\ell_{h}(b,j,a)+(P_{a}u_{h})(b)\} for every bb. Proof of Lemma 17.

For s≥1s\geq 1, set Δ​Nj,s:=Nj,s+1−Nj,s\Delta N_{j,s}:=N_{j,s+1}-N_{j,s}, order the labels completed in round ss by submission time, and expose them one at a time. =∑j=1K𝔼hπ​[Nj,t+1]​kl⁡(hj,h~j).\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{h}^{\pi}[N_{j,t+1}]\operatorname{kl}(h_{j},\widetilde{h}_{j}).

Since Nj,t+1≤Dj,t≤∑s=1t𝟏{Js=j}N_{j,t+1}\leq D_{j,t}\leq\sum_{s=1}^{t}\mathbf{1}\{J_{s}=j\} pathwise, 𝔼hπ​[Nj,t+1]≤𝔼hπ​[Dj,t]≤t​ωj\mathbb{E}_{h}^{\pi}[N_{j,t+1}]\leq\mathbb{E}_{h}^{\pi}[D_{j,t}]\leq t\omega_{j}, proving equation 72 and equation 73. ∎

For the following four lemmas, assume 0<μ<10<\mu<1, chold>0c_{\rm hold}>0, and τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1), and write m:=min⁡{τ,1−τ}m:=\min\{\tau,1-\tau\}. Choose an integer r≥1r\geq 1 that is a median of CtC_{t} conditional on Ct>0C_{t}>0, which exists since μ>0\mu>0, so that

uh​(b)≤𝔼bφ​[∑t=1τ0(ℓh​(Bt,Jt,At)−gh)],u_{h}(b)\leq\mathbb{E}_{b}^{\varphi}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{\tau_{0}}\bigl(\ell_{h}(B_{t},J_{t},A_{t})-g_{h}\bigr)\right], (104)

with equality when φ\varphi selects an ACOE-minimizing action at every state.

M¯h​(b)−M¯h​(0)≥∑c=1bρC​(c)​xh​(1)≥choldμ​ℙ​(1≤Ct≤b)≥chold2,\overline{M}^{h}(b)-\overline{M}^{h}(0)\geq\sum_{c=1}^{b}\rho_{C}(c)x_{h}(1)\geq\frac{c_{\rm hold}}{\mu}\mathbb{P}(1\leq C_{t}\leq b)\geq\frac{c_{\rm hold}}{2},

Lemma 22 (Empty-queue occupancy).

Appendix D Additional related work

D.1 Alternative self-confidence signals

Our experiments use the self-consistency score, i.e. the empirical mass of the largest answer class. This choice is natural when multiple responses are sampled, and answer consistency has previously been used as a signal to decide whether to escalate queries in LLM cascades (Yue et al., 2024). However, the deferral and learning components of our model do not depend on this particular definition of the score. They only require that queries be partitioned into levels Jt∈[K]J_{t}\in[K], each with an unknown conditional accuracy hj⋆=Pr⁡(Yt=1∣Jt=j)h_{j}^{\star}=\Pr(Y_{t}=1\mid J_{t}=j) that can be learned from selectively observed expert feedback. Thus, other scalar self-confidence measures can be substituted for self-consistency and discretized into levels before applying the same deferral framework. In particular, neither the deferral rule nor our analysis requires the self-confidence signal itself to be calibrated or the conditional accuracy to be monotone in that signal.

Sample-based self-confidence.

Let 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} denote the set of answer classes represented among the GG sampled responses, with empirical frequencies

qt,c:=1G∑g=1G𝟏{R^t,g∈c},c∈𝒞t.q_{t,c}:=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{R}_{t,g}\in c\},\qquad c\in\mathcal{C}_{t}.

Writing qt,(1)≥qt,(2)≥⋯q_{t,(1)}\geq q_{t,(2)}\geq\cdots for the ordered frequencies, with qt,(2)=0q_{t,(2)}=0 if |𝒞t|=1|\mathcal{C}_{t}|=1, the self-consistency score is simply qt,(1).q_{t,(1)}. It therefore retains only the empirical mass of the most frequent answer class.

A natural alternative is to use the entropy of the empirical answer distribution,

Ht:=−∑c∈𝒞tqt,clogqt,c.H_{t}:=-\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}q_{t,c}\log q_{t,c}.

which takes all sampled answer classes into account. For tasks with canonical answers, the classes can be defined directly by the extracted answer, yielding an entropy over answer labels. For open-ended tasks, responses can instead be grouped according to semantic equivalence, giving the discrete variant of semantic entropy (Kuhn et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024). Semantic entropy has also been considered directly as an uncertainty signal for LLM routing (Zhang et al., 2025).

Another simple alternative is the margin between the two most frequent answer classes,

qt,(1)−qt,(2),q_{t,(1)}-q_{t,(2)},

which measures how strongly the dominant answer is separated from its closest competitor. Margin-based self-confidence scores have been used to control escalation in language-model cascades (Ramírez et al., 2024). The statistic above applies the same principle directly to the empirical distribution of sampled answer classes.

For open-ended generation, self-confidence can also be estimated without first assigning responses to hard equivalence classes. Kernel Language Entropy (KLE) (Nikitin et al., 2024), for example, constructs a kernel from pairwise semantic similarities between sampled responses and measures uncertainty through its von Neumann entropy. Semantic voting (Jiang et al., 2026) also aggregates pairwise semantic similarities, using them to select responses for model self-improvement.

Model-internal self-confidence.

When model logits are available, self-confidence can instead be estimated from the predictive distributions produced during generation. For a generated response R^t=(r^t,1,…,r^t,Lt)\widehat{R}_{t}=(\widehat{r}_{t,1},\ldots,\widehat{r}_{t,L_{t}}), let

pt,ℓ:=Pr⁡(r^t,ℓ∣Xt,r^t,<ℓ)p_{t,\ell}:=\Pr(\widehat{r}_{t,\ell}\mid X_{t},\widehat{r}_{t,<\ell})

denote the probability assigned by the model to the generated token at position ℓ\ell. For example, Gupta et al. (2024) consider the sequence log-probability, which they refer to as the Chow-Sum,

Stsum:=∑ℓ=1Ltlog⁡pt,ℓ,S_{t}^{\mathrm{sum}}:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{t}}\log p_{t,\ell},

as a measure of model confidence. Since this score is affected by sequence length, they also consider the length-normalized Chow-Average score

Stavg:=1Lt​∑ℓ=1Ltlog⁡pt,ℓ.S_{t}^{\mathrm{avg}}:=\frac{1}{L_{t}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{t}}\log p_{t,\ell}.

These and other model-internal scores can be incorporated into our model by discretizing the resulting scalar self-confidence signal into levels and learning the corresponding conditional accuracies online.

These alternatives modify the self-confidence signal supplied to the deferral layer, but not the central learning problem studied in this work. In all cases, the system must learn from delayed and selectively observed feedback which score levels are sufficiently reliable to accept, while simultaneously accounting for the state-dependent cost of expert intervention.

D.2 Probabilistic calibration

Calibration is the property that characterizes the relationship between a model’s confidence scores and the probability that its predictions are correct: a confidence score is calibrated if predictions assigned confidence pp are correct with probability pp. Classical post-hoc calibration methods include histogram binning (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2001), Platt scaling (Platt, 1999), isotonic regression (Robertson et al., 1988; Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002). In our problem, the conditional accuracies are learned from delayed, selectively observed human feedback, and learning is evaluated through deferral regret rather than calibration error.

D.3 Additional learning-to-defer formulations

Charusaie et al. (2022) study learning predictors that complement humans and develop active learning schemes to reduce the number of expert predictions required during training. In our model, expert feedback is instead acquired during deployment to learn the conditional accuracies of a fixed LLM.

Learning to defer with multiple experts.

Building on the single-expert setting, learning to defer has been generalized to multiple heterogeneous experts whose competencies may vary across inputs. In this setting, the learner must determine not only whether to defer, but also which expert should handle each instance. Early multi-expert formulations jointly learned a predictive model and an allocation rule while accounting for heterogeneous expert competencies and, in some cases, expert biases and fairness considerations (Keswani et al., 2021; Hemmer et al., 2022). Subsequent work developed more principled formulations for expert selection, including calibrated and consistent surrogate objectives (Verma et al., 2023). A complementary line of work has focused on the theoretical foundations of multi-expert deferral. Mao et al. (2023) study the two-stage setting, in which a predictor is fixed and a deferral function is learned to select among experts, while Mao et al. (2024a) develop surrogate losses with realizable HH-consistency, HH-consistency, and Bayes-consistency guarantees. More recently, Mao et al. (2025) provide a unified treatment of single-stage and two-stage multi-expert deferral and establish stronger consistency guarantees for both settings. Other extensions consider learning with limited expert annotations (Hemmer et al., 2023), adaptation to previously unseen experts (Tailor et al., 2024), regression (Mao et al., 2024b), imbalanced expert data (Cortes et al., 2026), and Top-kk deferral, where multiple experts may be selected for the same instance (Montreuil et al., 2026).

D.4 LLM routing

FrugalGPT constructs LLM cascades to reduce monetary cost while maintaining predictive quality (Chen et al., 2024). RouteLLM learns routers between stronger and weaker models using preference data (Ong et al., 2025). Jitkrittum et al. (2026) introduce UniRoute, a model-routing framework that represents LLMs through their prediction-error profiles on representative prompts, thus enabling cost-aware routing to previously unseen models without retraining the router. These methods allocate computation among automated models. We first sample from a fixed LLM, then decide whether to defer to a capacity-constrained human expert whose completed reviews supply ground-truth labels.

D.5 Structured admission control

Queue-aware learning has also been studied through structured admission-control policies. In particular, UCRL-AC (Weber et al., 2024) exploits the structure of multi-class admission control to obtain sharper worst-case regret guarantees than generic MDP approaches, while SALMUT (Roy et al., 2021) assumes that the optimal policy has an ordered multi-threshold structure and directly learns the corresponding vector of class-specific thresholds using stochastic approximation. The learning problems differ substantially from ours. In Weber et al. (2024), arrival rates are unknown and are learned passively from exogenously observed arrivals, while the class-dependent reward model is known. Roy et al. (2021) allows the transition dynamics to be unknown, but learns from state, reward, and transition observations generated by interaction with the system. In our model, by contrast, the confidence level-dependent cost of accepting the LLM answer is itself unknown since it depends on the unknown conditional accuracy vector, and it is learned only through queries deferred to the expert. Thus, obtaining information about prediction quality requires consuming expert capacity and increasing queue congestion, with the resulting feedback additionally delayed by expert service.

D.6 Active learning and oracle queries

Active learning studies how a learner can selectively acquire costly labels while maintaining predictive performance (Dasgupta, 2011; Hanneke, 2014). Online variants require these query decisions to be made sequentially under partial feedback (Hao et al., 2018). Réveillard et al. (2026) study online classification in which costly expert consultations provide labeled examples used to improve subsequent predictions. In our model, the LLM remains fixed, and expert feedback instead estimates conditional accuracies to guide deferral. Russo et al. (2024) study a limited budget of best-action queries, which reveal the identity of the best action before the current decision. This information differs from our completed-review labels, which reveal whether the LLM response was correct without revealing the optimal deferral decision.

D.7 Human–AI decision support

Related work studies how the relationship between human and AI confidence affects the usefulness of AI advice (Corvelo Benz and Rodriguez, 2023; Corvelo Benz and Gomez Rodriguez, 2025). Benz et al. (2026) study learning decision policies through repeated interactions under human-alignment and full feedback. In our model, an accepted LLM response provides no correctness feedback, and expert review is limited by queue capacity.

Appendix E Datasets

E.1 Synthetic datasets

In this section, we describe the two synthetic instances used in Appendix G. Both have K=10K=10 self-confidence levels and are shown in Figure 5.

Two-point instance.

The first instance uses the two-point family hj⋆∈{0.5−δ,0.5+δ}h^{\star}_{j}\in\{0.5-\delta,0.5+\delta\}, j∈[K]j\in[K], with uniform arrival rates ωj=1/K\omega_{j}=1/K (top panel of Figure 5). This construction is motivated by the hard instances used in the proof of our minimax lower bound (Theorem 4): under immediate service (μ=1\mu=1), uniform arrivals and cexp/ce=1/2c_{\rm exp}/c_{e}=1/2, the oracle threshold is τ=1/2\tau=1/2, and if K≤TK\leq T, these instances take hj⋆∈{τ−δ,τ+δ}h^{\star}_{j}\in\{\tau-\delta,\tau+\delta\} with δ=18​K/T\delta=\frac{1}{8}\sqrt{K/T}. Appendix G.1 uses this instance in that setting only, with δ\delta as a free parameter.

Monotone instance.

The second instance combines increasing conditional accuracies h⋆=(.04,.13,.23,.33,.43,.54,.64,.75,.86,.94)h^{\star}=(.04,.13,.23,.33,.43,.54,.64,.75,.86,.94) with arrival rates concentrated on the high levels (bottom panel of Figure 5). Since the scores are pj=(j−1)/9p_{j}=(j-1)/9, they are nearly calibrated: this instance models an LLM that is slightly underconfident at the three lowest levels and overconfident at the others, by at most 0.060.06. Since the conditional accuracies span most of [0,1][0,1], the oracle threshold falls between the accuracies of two levels for a wide range of service rates, costs and queue sizes. This ensures the optimal actions do not become trivial to learn when we vary these parameters, unless deferral is never worthwhile (cexp≥cec_{\rm exp}\geq c_{e}). We use this instance in Appendix G.2, where we vary the service rate μ\mu, the expert cost cexpc_{\rm exp} and the holding cost choldc_{\rm hold}, with the conditional accuracies held fixed.

E.2 Real-world datasets

In this section, we describe the datasets used in our real-world experiments. We start from three question-answering datasets with verifiable answers:

  • •

    GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) contains grade-school math problems with numerical answers. We use all 8,7928{,}792 questions from its train and test splits.

  • •

    NuminaMath-TIR (Li et al., 2024) contains competition-style mathematics problems. We use its first 10,00010{,}000 training questions, from which we remove 157157 exact duplicates and 659659 questions that also appear in GSM8K, leaving 9,1849{,}184.

  • •

    MedMCQA is a large-scale medical dataset derived primarily from medical entrance and professional examinations (Pal et al., 2022). It contains multiple-choice questions with four options. We use all 187,005187{,}005 questions of its train and validation splits.

We use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-0.6B, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025a; Qwen et al., 2025), and sample 2020 answers per question. Answers are sampled with vLLM at temperature 0.60.6 and top-pp 0.950.95, without top-kk truncation, with up to 2,0482{,}048 generated tokens per answer and a maximum model sequence length (prompt plus output) of 4,0964{,}096 tokens.

Answer extraction and grading.

A final answer is extracted from each generation by taking the last complete <answer> block. If none is present, we use a terminal \boxed{} expression or an explicit final-answer declaration. Otherwise, no answer is returned. Answers are grouped into equivalence classes, either by mathematical equivalence with Math-Verify (Hugging Face, 2025) for the math datasets, which handles fractions, radicals, tuples, sets and symbolic expressions, or by option letter for MedMCQA. The same equivalence decides whether Rt≡Rt⋆R_{t}\equiv R^{\star}_{t}. Ties between the largest classes are broken by first occurrence. Generations without an extractable answer count in the denominator of the score but cast no vote, so a question on which no generation yields an answer has score 00 and Yt=0Y_{t}=0. Questions whose ground-truth answer could not be parsed, or whose grading timed out, are removed: 5858 NuminaMath questions for the Qwen3 models, and 8585 NuminaMath and 1212 GSM8K questions for Qwen2.5-0.5B.

Instances.

Figure 6 shows h⋆h^{\star} and ω\omega for all (dataset, LLM) pairs, from which the instances are built as in Section 6. The regimes of Figure 2 extend to Qwen2.5-0.5B: its conditional accuracy is above the score on the math datasets, especially on GSM8K, and varies little with the score on MedMCQA. Across all three datasets, the self-consistency score is generally not calibrated, i.e. h⋆≠ph^{\star}\neq p. Moreover, h⋆h^{\star} generally is not monotone in the self-consistency level jj. This motivates learning h⋆h^{\star} rather than assuming the score is calibrated.

Appendix F Baselines and implementation details

The costs (ce,cexp,chold)(c_{e},c_{\rm exp},c_{\rm hold}), the service distribution ρC\rho_{C} and the queue capacity B¯\bar{B} are known to all algorithms. In the synthetic experiments, ω\omega is known. In the real-world experiments it is unknown, and every learning algorithm that needs it uses the empirical frequencies ω^j,t=Oj,t/t\hat{\omega}_{j,t}=O_{j,t}/t, where Oj,t=∑s≤t𝟏{Js=j}O_{j,t}=\sum_{s\leq t}\mathbf{1}\{J_{s}=j\} counts the arrivals at self-confidence level jj up to round tt. Let Nj,tN_{j,t} and Cj,tC_{j,t} be the number of level-jj labels received before the decision of round tt and the number of correct ones among them, and h^j,Nj,t=(Cj,t/Nj,t)𝟏{Nj,t>0}\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}}=(C_{j,t}/N_{j,t})\mathbf{1}\{N_{j,t}>0\} their empirical mean.

Plug-in algorithms (KL-PBD, KL-PBD+, GBD, NBD).

These four algorithms share the decision rule of KL-PBD, At=𝟏{ce(1−hJt,t)>Mtht(Bt)}A_{t}=\mathbf{1}\{c_{e}(1-h_{J_{t},t})>M^{h_{t}}_{t}(B_{t})\}, and differ only in the conditional accuracy vector hth_{t} plugged into the marginal cost of deferral MthtM^{h_{t}}_{t}:

  • •

    KL-PBD: the KL lower confidence bound h¯j,t\underline{h}_{j,t} with confidence budget ϕ⁡(T)=log⁡T+log⁡log⁡T\phi(T)=\log T+\log\log T;

  • •

    KL-PBD+: the same bound with the level-dependent budget log⁡(Oj,t/Nj,t)\log(O_{j,t}/N_{j,t}) in place of ϕ⁡(T)\phi(T), in the spirit of the KL-UCB+ family of algorithms (Garivier and Cappé, 2011; Achab et al., 2018);

  • •

    GBD (Greedy Bellman Deferral): the empirical mean h^j,Nj,t\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}};

  • •

    NBD (Naive Bellman Deferral): the surrogate h=ph=p, i.e. the score is taken as calibrated and nothing is learned about h⋆h^{\star}.

With known ω\omega, the finite-horizon recursion is re-solved whenever a new label arrives (never for NBD). With unknown ω\omega, it is re-solved at every round with the current (ht,ω^t)(h_{t},\hat{\omega}_{t}), for NBD included. The marginal costs are computed exactly by backward induction over the remaining horizon, with the terminal draining cost D⁡(b)D(b) of Section 3.

Fixed-threshold policies (FCT, FQT).

Fixed Confidence Threshold defers iff pJt<τconfp_{J_{t}}<\tau^{\rm conf}; Fixed Queue Threshold defers iff Bt<τJtqueueB_{t}<\tau^{\rm queue}_{J_{t}} for a threshold vector τqueue∈{0,…,B¯}K\tau^{\rm queue}\in\{0,\ldots,\bar{B}\}^{K}. Both are tuned once before the run to minimize the expected cost under the surrogate h=ph=p, computed exactly by dynamic programming. When ω\omega is unknown the uniform distribution ωj=1/K\omega_{j}=1/K is used in place of ω\omega. Since only the ordering of {p1,…,pK}\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{K}\} matters for FCT, its K+1K+1 candidate policies are enumerated exhaustively. For FQT, exhaustive search over {0,…,B¯}K\{0,\ldots,\bar{B}\}^{K} is infeasible, so we use coordinate descent: each threshold τjqueue\tau_{j}^{\rm queue} is optimized over {0,…,B¯}\{0,\ldots,\bar{B}\} with the others fixed, cycling over j=1,…,Kj=1,\ldots,K until the vector no longer changes. We run this from several deterministic initializations and keep the best result, which need not be the global optimum.

SALMUT-SF.

We adapt SALMUT (Roy et al., 2021), which defers a level-jj query iff Bt<τjB_{t}<\tau_{j}, with one queue threshold τj∈[0,B¯]\tau_{j}\in[0,\bar{B}] per level, initialized at τj=0\tau_{j}=0. In the setting of Roy et al. (2021), hh would be known. In our case, we estimate it with h^j,Nj,t\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}}. Let b=Btb=B_{t}, j=Jtj=J_{t}, a=Ata=A_{t} and b′=Bt+1b^{\prime}=B_{t+1}. At the end of round tt, after service and label processing, the relative-value critic, initialized at V⁡(b)=0V(b)=0, is updated at the pre-decision queue state bb, including when b=B¯b=\bar{B}, with step size αnb=(⌊nb/100⌋+2)−0.6\alpha_{n_{b}}=(\lfloor n_{b}/100\rfloor+2)^{-0.6} where nbn_{b} counts the updates at state bb:

V⁡(b)←V⁡(b)+αnb​[chold​b+cexp​a+ce​(1−h^j,Nj,t+1)​(1−a)+V⁡(b′)−V⁡(0)−V⁡(b)].V(b)\leftarrow V(b)+\alpha_{n_{b}}\bigl[c_{\rm hold}b+c_{\rm exp}a+c_{e}(1-\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t+1}})(1-a)+V(b^{\prime})-V(0)-V(b)\bigr].

For the actor, we retain SALMUT’s sigmoid interpolation f⁡(b,τ)=1/(1+e−(b−τ−1/2))f(b,\tau)=1/(1+e^{-(b-\tau-1/2)}). Note that unlike Roy et al. (2021), the transition probabilities are assumed known in our setting, so they do not need to be estimated. Therefore, after the critic update, for b<B¯b<\bar{B}, we estimate the advantage function via the updated critic, Q^1−Q^0=cexp−ce​(1−h^j,Nj,t+1)+(P1​V)​(b)−(P0​V)​(b)\hat{Q}_{1}-\hat{Q}_{0}=c_{\rm exp}-c_{e}(1-\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t+1}})+(P_{1}V)(b)-(P_{0}V)(b), where (Pa​V)​(b)=∑b′Pa​(b,b′)​V​(b′)(P_{a}V)(b)=\sum_{b^{\prime}}P_{a}(b,b^{\prime})V(b^{\prime}), and for b<B¯b<\bar{B} we update the threshold of the arriving level as

τj←Π[0,B¯]​[τj−10t+100​f​(b,τj)​(1−f⁡(b,τj))​(Q^1−Q^0)].\tau_{j}\leftarrow\Pi_{[0,\bar{B}]}\Bigl[\tau_{j}-\tfrac{10}{t+100}\,f(b,\tau_{j})\bigl(1-f(b,\tau_{j})\bigr)(\hat{Q}_{1}-\hat{Q}_{0})\Bigr].

We do not use SALMUT’s ordering constraint on the thresholds, since conditional accuracies need not be ordered in the score. When the threshold rule accepts, we force a feasible deferral with probability εt=min⁡{.5, 2/t}\varepsilon_{t}=\min\{.5,\,2/\sqrt{t}\}; without it a level can stop producing the labels needed to revise an optimistic threshold due to the selective nature of the feedback in our problem (this failure mode is explored in Appendix H.5). The same hyperparameters are used in every instance.

Queue-unaware bandit algorithms (KL-UCB-4P, KL-UCB+-4P).

Under immediate service (μ=1\mu=1), the queue stays empty and Mt​(0)=cexpM_{t}(0)=c_{\rm exp}. The problem then reduces to a separate learning task for each self-confidence level: at each round the level Jt=jJ_{t}=j is revealed and the learner faces a two-armed bandit with one known arm. Indeed, one can equivalently subtract the cost ce​(1−Yt)c_{e}(1-Y_{t}) of accepting from both actions, so that accepting has reward 00, while deferring has reward ce​(1−Yt)−cexpc_{e}(1-Y_{t})-c_{\rm exp}, with unknown mean ce​(1−hj⋆)−cexpc_{e}(1-h^{\star}_{j})-c_{\rm exp}, observed only when the query is deferred. This is close to the profitable-bandit problem of Achab et al. (2018), played independently at each level, which motivates a comparison with their algorithms. We adapt their algorithms to our setting, so that they defer iff ce​q¯j,t≥cexpc_{e}\bar{q}_{j,t}\geq c_{\rm exp}, ignoring the queue except when it is full, where q¯j,t\bar{q}_{j,t} is the KL upper confidence bound on the LLM error probability 1−hj⋆1-h^{\star}_{j}, computed from 1−h^j,Nj,t1-\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}} with budget log⁡Oj,t+3​log⁡log⁡Oj,t\log O_{j,t}+3\log\log O_{j,t} for KL-UCB-4P and log⁡(Oj,t/Nj,t)\log(O_{j,t}/N_{j,t}) for KL-UCB+-4P, using the level clock Oj,tO_{j,t} in place of tt, with unlabeled levels having q¯j,t=1\bar{q}_{j,t}=1 so that they are deferred. Equivalently, up to ties, they follow the decision rule of KL-PBD with Mtht​(Bt)M^{h_{t}}_{t}(B_{t}) replaced by cexpc_{\rm exp}, its value under immediate service: KL-UCB+-4P is then KL-PBD+, and KL-UCB-4P is KL-PBD with budget log⁡Oj,t+3​log⁡log⁡Oj,t\log O_{j,t}+3\log\log O_{j,t} in place of ϕ⁡(T)\phi(T). When μ<1\mu<1, labels arrive only once a deferred query is served, and the algorithms use the labels available at each round.

Simulation protocol.

For every run, all algorithms see the same arrivals (Jt)(J_{t}), latent labels (Yt)(Y_{t}) and service capacities (Ct)(C_{t}), and keep separate first-in, first-out (FIFO) queues. A label completed after the decision of round tt is available from round t+1t+1. We compute the regret as R^T=∑t≤T,Bt<B¯|L⋆(Jt)−Mt⋆(Bt)|𝟏{At≠At⋆}\hat{R}_{T}=\sum_{t\leq T,\,B_{t}<\bar{B}}|L^{\star}(J_{t})-M^{\star}_{t}(B_{t})|\mathbf{1}\{A_{t}\neq A^{\star}_{t}\} (Lemma 2), averaged over independent runs with pointwise 95%95\% normal confidence intervals. The code used for our experiments is provided in the supplementary files.

Appendix G Synthetic experiments

G.1 Effect of KK and of the oracle gap on KL-PBD regret

In this experiment, we examine how the number of levels, the separation between the accuracies and the oracle threshold, and the arrival distribution ω\omega affect KL-PBD’s regret. We use the two-point instance of Appendix E.1 (top row of Figure 5) with μ=1\mu=1, ce=1c_{e}=1 and cexp=0.5c_{\rm exp}=0.5, so that the oracle threshold is τ=1/2\tau=1/2: the oracle defers the levels jj with hj⋆=0.5−δh^{\star}_{j}=0.5-\delta and accepts those with hj⋆=0.5+δh^{\star}_{j}=0.5+\delta. All experiments use T=2⋅105T=2\cdot 10^{5} and 100100 runs.

Figure 7 shows that regret increases with KK, since the learner must acquire more expert feedback to identify the correct action in a larger number of levels. The dependence on δ\delta reflects the usual gap-dependent learning trade-off. Larger gaps make an incorrect deferral more costly initially, but they are statistically easier to distinguish from the oracle threshold, so the learner identifies the optimal action sooner and the regret curves flatten earlier. Conversely, when δ\delta is small, the conditional accuracies lie closer to the threshold and require substantially more feedback to distinguish, leading to larger regret over the range of the figure.

Under immediate service, KL-PBD defers level jj until Nj,t​kl​(h^j,Nj,t,1/2)≥ϕ⁡(T)N_{j,t}\,\mathrm{kl}(\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}},1/2)\geq\phi(T). A level with hj⋆=0.5+δh^{\star}_{j}=0.5+\delta therefore needs about ϕ⁡(T)/(2​δ2)\phi(T)/(2\delta^{2}) labels before it is accepted, each deferral costing δ\delta, while a level with hj⋆=0.5−δh^{\star}_{j}=0.5-\delta is deferred, as by the oracle. Each level above the threshold thus contributes about min⁡{δ​ωj​T,ϕ⁡(T)/(2​δ)}\min\{\delta\,\omega_{j}T,\ \phi(T)/(2\delta)\} to the regret.

Table 1 complements Figure 7 by reporting the final regret at T=2⋅105T=2\cdot 10^{5}. The results show that regret increases significantly with KK, confirming the additional learning burden associated with a larger number of levels. At δ=0.08\delta=0.08, every oracle decision is learned well before TT, and each level above the threshold adds about ϕ⁡(T)/(2​δ)≈90\phi(T)/(2\delta)\approx 90 to the regret. For every value of KK except K=50K=50, regret decreases as δ\delta increases; we explain the exception below.

Table 2 further illustrates the non-monotone dependence of finite-horizon regret on the oracle gap δ\delta. For very small δ\delta, distinguishing which side of the oracle threshold the accuracy is requires many observations, but the regret incurred by an incorrect decision is itself only O⁡(δ)O(\delta), so the regret is at most of order δ​T\delta T. In this case, KL-PBD does not have enough time to learn the oracle decisions, and RT≈δ​T/2R_{T}\approx\delta T/2. For larger δ\delta, the levels are statistically easier to distinguish and the regret decreases roughly as K​ϕ​(T)/(4​δ)K\phi(T)/(4\delta). Consequently, the largest regret is observed near the crossover between these two regimes, δ⋆=ϕ⁡(T)​K/(2​T)≈0.019\delta^{\star}=\sqrt{\phi(T)K/(2T)}\approx 0.019 for K=10K=10. Since δ⋆\delta^{\star} grows with KK (δ⋆≈0.043\delta^{\star}\approx 0.043 for K=50K=50), the regret for K=50K=50 is lower at δ=0.02\delta=0.02 than at δ=0.04\delta=0.04 (Table 1).

The right panel examines the effect of non-uniform arrivals with K=10K=10. We parameterize

ω1=1K+ρ(1−1K),ωj=1−ρK,j=2,…,K,\omega_{1}=\frac{1}{K}+\rho\left(1-\frac{1}{K}\right),\qquad\omega_{j}=\frac{1-\rho}{K},\quad j=2,\ldots,K,

so that ρ=0\rho=0 corresponds to uniform arrivals and increasing ρ\rho concentrates probability mass on a single level. We set hj⋆=0.5+δjh^{\star}_{j}=0.5+\delta_{j} with δj=ϕ⁡(T)/(2​ωj​T)\delta_{j}=\sqrt{\phi(T)/(2\omega_{j}T)} for every level. Unlike in the two-point instance, all levels lie above the threshold: a level below it is deferred by both KL-PBD and the oracle and adds no regret, so this makes every level contribute. Level jj receives about ωj​T\omega_{j}T arrivals and needs about ϕ⁡(T)/(2​δj2)=ωj​T\phi(T)/(2\delta_{j}^{2})=\omega_{j}T labels before it is accepted, so with this gap KL-PBD starts accepting level jj at about the horizon. For uniform arrivals, δj=δ⋆\delta_{j}=\delta^{\star}. Each level then contributes about δj​ωj​T=ϕ⁡(T)​ωj​T/2\delta_{j}\,\omega_{j}T=\sqrt{\phi(T)\,\omega_{j}T/2} to the regret. Regret is largest under the uniform distribution and decreases as the arrival mass becomes more concentrated. This ordering is consistent with the dependence on ω\omega in Theorem 2, whose leading term is O~​(T​∑j=1Kωj)\widetilde{O}\bigl(\sqrt{T}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\sqrt{\omega_{j}}\bigr) and is maximized when ωj=1/K\omega_{j}=1/K for j∈[K]j\in[K]. Quantitatively, RT/(T​∑j=1Kωj)R_{T}/(\sqrt{T}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\sqrt{\omega_{j}}) stays between 2.212.21 and 2.292.29 for all ρ\rho.

G.2 Effect of service rate and cost parameters

In this experiment we use the monotone instance (bottom row of Figure 5) in order to evaluate how KL-PBD is affected by the expert service rate. We set the queue capacity to B¯=20\bar{B}=20, the LLM error cost to ce=2c_{e}=2, the expert-review cost to cexp=0.25c_{\rm exp}=0.25, and the holding cost to chold=0.1c_{\rm hold}=0.1. We vary the expert service rate over μ∈{0.2,0.4,0.5,0.6,0.8,1.0}\mu\in\{0.2,0.4,0.5,0.6,0.8,1.0\}, where in each round the expert completes a pending query with probability μ\mu.

For each service rate, we run the system for T=50,000T=50{,}000 rounds and average results over 20 independent runs. We report the average queue size, the cumulative regret relative to the oracle, the response accuracy, i.e., the fraction of queries answered correctly, counting deferred queries as correct, and the average threshold, i.e., the time average of τ^t​(Bt)\widehat{\tau}_{t}(B_{t}).

Table 3 shows that increasing the expert service rate generally makes deferral more attractive. As μ\mu increases, deferred queries are processed more quickly, reducing the congestion cost associated with sending additional jobs to the expert. Consistent with this behavior, the average threshold increases from 0.26630.2663 at μ=0.2\mu=0.2 to 0.8750=1−cexp/ce0.8750=1-c_{\rm exp}/c_{e} at μ=1.0\mu=1.0, while response accuracy improves substantially from 0.77100.7710 to 0.99370.9937. The average queue size remains below one across all service rates, falls from 0.740.74 at μ=0.5\mu=0.5 to 0.370.37 at μ=0.8\mu=0.8, and reaches zero at μ=1.0\mu=1.0, where deferred jobs are cleared immediately.

Cumulative regret remains non-monotone in μ\mu, ranging from 80.6180.61 to 301.17301.17 across the tested service rates. In particular, regret is relatively high at μ=0.4\mu=0.4 and reaches its maximum at μ=0.8\mu=0.8, despite the corresponding improvements in response accuracy and queue length. This reflects the fact that each service rate induces a different control problem and oracle policy. At μ=1.0\mu=1.0, the experiment attains both its highest response accuracy, 0.99370.9937, and its lowest cumulative regret, 80.6180.61.

Figure 8 (right) shows the policy learned by KL-PBD at t=T/2t=T/2. It exhibits a clear threshold structure: within each level, the action changes from defer to accept once the queue size exceeds a level-dependent boundary, producing the staircase-shaped frontier visible across all panels. As the expert service rate μ\mu increases, the defer region expands toward larger queue sizes, since a faster expert clears deferred requests more quickly.

Figure 8 (left) shows how the KL-PBD threshold τ^t​(b)\widehat{\tau}_{t}(b) varies with the current queue size for different expert service rates. For every value of μ\mu, the threshold decreases as the queue grows, reflecting the increasing congestion cost of sending additional queries to the expert. Once the queue becomes sufficiently large, the threshold reaches zero, and no query is deferred. Increasing the service rate shifts the threshold curve upward and extends it over larger queue sizes. When the expert is slow, as for μ=0.2\mu=0.2, the threshold falls rapidly and reaches zero at a small queue size. In contrast, faster service allows the system to tolerate substantially more queued queries before the threshold becomes small.

We then fix μ=0.5\mu=0.5 and vary the holding cost chold∈{0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5}c_{\rm hold}\in\{0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5\} with cexp=0.25c_{\rm exp}=0.25, and the expert-review cost cexp∈{0,0.25,1,3}c_{\rm exp}\in\{0,0.25,1,3\} with chold=0.05c_{\rm hold}=0.05, over 10 independent runs of T=50,000T=50{,}000 rounds. In these sweeps, the thresholds of KL-PBD are recomputed after every 50 changes of the lower bounds.

Table 4 shows that the holding cost and expert-review cost affect KL-PBD in distinct ways. With cexp=0.25c_{\mathrm{exp}}=0.25, increasing choldc_{\mathrm{hold}} from 0.0050.005 to 0.50.5 reduces the mean queue from 2.842.84 to 0.230.23 and the deferral rate from 49.62%49.62\% to 22.90%22.90\%. As fewer queries are routed to the expert, response accuracy decreases from 91.27%91.27\% to 81.06%81.06\%. The average threshold decreases overall from 0.6350.635 to 0.4290.429. Regret is non-monotone because changing choldc_{\mathrm{hold}} also changes the oracle policy.

The expert-review-cost sweep exhibits a sharper transition. With chold=0.05c_{\mathrm{hold}}=0.05, increasing cexpc_{\mathrm{exp}} from 00 to 11 reduces the mean queue from 1.221.22 to 0.260.26, the deferral rate from 48.72%48.72\% to 18.71%18.71\%, and response accuracy from 89.97%89.97\% to 80.20%80.20\%; the average threshold correspondingly decreases from 0.6110.611 to 0.4410.441. For cexp≥3c_{\mathrm{exp}}\geq 3, KL-PBD does not defer, and the accuracy of 67.83%67.83\% is the LLM-only accuracy. This is due to the choice of cost parameters: the expected cost ce​(1−hJt⋆)≤ce=2c_{e}(1-h^{\star}_{J_{t}})\leq c_{e}=2 of accepting the LLM response is below the expert-review cost, so both KL-PBD and the oracle accept every query, yielding zero regret.

Figure 9 demonstrates how the expert-review cost cexpc_{\mathrm{exp}} governs the operating regime of KL-PBD. For cexp∈{0,0.25}c_{\mathrm{exp}}\in\{0,0.25\}, expert review remains sufficiently inexpensive that the policy defers a large fraction of arriving queries, thereby maintaining a high accepted-LLM accuracy. As cexpc_{\mathrm{exp}} increases to 11, the policy becomes substantially more selective: the deferral rate decreases, more queries are answered directly by the LLM, and the accuracy of the accepted LLM responses decreases because LLM answers are also accepted at lower confidence levels. For cexp≥3c_{\mathrm{exp}}\geq 3, expert review is no longer used, and the accepted-LLM accuracy equals the LLM accuracy.

The cumulative-regret trajectories show that the intermediate-cost regime is the most challenging. At cexp=1c_{\mathrm{exp}}=1, expert review is still optimal in a substantial set of level–queue states, but less frequent deferrals slow the acquisition of informative expert feedback. Consequently, regret is substantially larger than for cexp∈{0,0.25}c_{\mathrm{exp}}\in\{0,0.25\}. The second row makes the underlying mechanism explicit. Increasing cexpc_{\mathrm{exp}} reduces the number of completed expert labels, lowers the average queue size, and shifts the threshold τ^T/2​(b)\widehat{\tau}_{T/2}(b) downward.

Figure 10 illustrates the behavior shown in Table 4 over time: as choldc_{\mathrm{hold}} increases, maintaining backlog becomes more expensive, so the policy becomes increasingly selective and a larger fraction of queries is answered directly by the LLM. It also shows that the reduction in expert use limits the feedback available for learning: at low holding costs, roughly half of all queries, about 2.5×1042.5\times 10^{4}, yield completed expert labels, compared with only about 1.1×1041.1\times 10^{4} at chold=0.5c_{\mathrm{hold}}=0.5. The threshold curves provide the state-level view: for every choldc_{\mathrm{hold}}, τ^T/2​(b)\widehat{\tau}_{T/2}(b) decreases with backlog, with the decline becoming markedly steeper as the holding cost increases. In particular, the threshold reaches zero at moderate backlog for chold=0.1c_{\mathrm{hold}}=0.1 and almost immediately for chold=0.5c_{\mathrm{hold}}=0.5, showing that higher holding costs make the deferral rule increasingly sensitive to congestion.

Figure 11 shows how the learned KL-PBD deferral policy changes as the expert-review and holding costs increase. In both sweeps, higher costs make deferral less attractive, so the deferral region progressively shrinks: the yellow defer region contracts while the purple accept region expands, indicating that the policy relies increasingly on the LLM and sends fewer queries to the expert.

Appendix H Additional real-world experiments and details

This section extends the experiments of Section 6. We first report the regret of all algorithms on the instances of Section 6 and on additional Qwen2.5-0.5B instances, and in a separate experiment, we report how the final regret grows with the horizon. We then vary the service rate to show the benefit of queue awareness, and compare the policy learned by KL-PBD with the oracle policy. Finally, we show how selective feedback makes GBD fail, which illustrates the need for pessimism. Unless stated otherwise, the setting is that of Section 6. Implementation details are given in Appendix F.

H.1 Regret of all algorithms

Table 5 and Figure 12 report the regret of all algorithms described in Appendix F on all instances. KL-PBD+ has the lowest regret in 88 of the 99 instances. The exception is Qwen2.5-0.5B on NuminaMath, where the score is nearly calibrated and NBD (102102) is still below KL-PBD+ (115115) at T=105T=10^{5}; a longer horizon is needed for KL-PBD+ to overtake NBD in this instance, as we show in Table 6. The queue-unaware algorithms KL-UCB-4P and KL-UCB+-4P incur 2424 to 450450 times the regret of KL-PBD+ on eight instances. KL-UCB+-4P is only competitive on Qwen3-4B GSM8K, where the LLM accuracy averages 95%95\%, which makes deferral rare and the queue almost always empty. FCT is the worst of the three h=ph=p surrogate algorithms on every instance.

H.2 Regret as a function of the horizon

Figure 13 and Table 6 report the final regret when the horizon varies in T∈{104,5⋅104,105,2⋅105}T\in\{10^{4},5\cdot 10^{4},10^{5},2\cdot 10^{5}\}, averaged over 24 runs per horizon. The regret of GBD and of the algorithms using the h=ph=p surrogate grows linearly in TT, by a factor of about 1010 from T=104T=10^{4} to 10510^{5}, whereas that of KL-PBD and KL-PBD+ grows by a factor between 1.61.6 and 4.44.4. SALMUT-SF lies in between, with a factor between 3.43.4 and 6.86.8.

H.3 Service rate and queue-unaware algorithms

We rerun the Qwen3-4B MedMCQA instance with service rates μ∈{.2,.35,.5,.7,1}\mu\in\{.2,.35,.5,.7,1\}, T=5⋅104T=5\cdot 10^{4} and 2424 runs, with FCT and FQT retuned for each μ\mu (Figure 14 and Table 7). At μ=1\mu=1 the queue stays empty and Mt​(0)=cexpM_{t}(0)=c_{\rm exp}. The regret of queue-aware and queue-unaware algorithms then coincides pairwise, KL-PBD+ with KL-UCB+-4P (41.941.9) and NBD with FCT and FQT (2,5112{,}511), while KL-PBD and KL-UCB-4P differ in regret only due to the difference in their confidence budgets (113113 against 158158). For μ<1\mu<1, KL-UCB-4P and KL-UCB+-4P keep deferring regardless of the queue: at μ=.2\mu=.2 it is full in 4141 to 56%56\% of the rounds, and their regret exceeds 200200 times that of KL-PBD+. The regret of KL-PBD and KL-PBD+ varies by less than a factor 22 across μ\mu. The regret of NBD grows with μ\mu, since a faster expert makes deferral optimal at more levels, which the surrogate h=ph=p misses. FCT and FQT follow the same trend up to μ=.7\mu=.7, with an additional cost from their restricted form, which vanishes at μ=1\mu=1: the optimal rule under h=ph=p is then a fixed confidence cutoff, which both can represent, so they recover the decisions of NBD.

H.4 Learned threshold and decisions

The top row of Figure 15 shows the threshold and decisions learned by KL-PBD for Qwen3-0.6B at t=T/2t=T/2, from one run for each μ\mu, in the format of Figure 4: the threshold τ^t​(b)=1−Mth¯t​(b)/ce\widehat{\tau}_{t}(b)=1-M^{\underline{h}_{t}}_{t}(b)/c_{e} (top) and the decisions 𝟏{h¯j,t<τ^t(b)}\mathbf{1}\{\underline{h}_{j,t}<\widehat{\tau}_{t}(b)\} for μ=0.35\mu=0.35 (bottom). The learned thresholds are within 0.090.09 of the oracle ones for every μ\mu. The learned decisions differ from the oracle’s due to extra deferrals caused by KL-PBD’s pessimism. For example, at b=2b=2 on MedMCQA, KL-PBD defers queries with scores up to 30%30\% whereas the oracle accepts those with scores higher than 5%5\%. The difference is larger for Qwen3-4B (middle and bottom rows of Figure 15). Since this LLM is more accurate, it is deferred less, so by t=T/2t=T/2 KL-PBD has collected fewer labels (2,6492{,}649 on GSM8K against 9,9019{,}901 for Qwen3-0.6B). Its lower confidence bounds are consequently looser, and it keeps deferring levels at intermediate queue sizes where the oracle no longer does (b=3b=3 to 66 on GSM8K, b=2b=2 to 55 on MedMCQA). On GSM8K, the levels still deferred at b=7b=7 are those with at most 2020 labels, which produces the isolated cells in the bottom row.

H.5 The importance of pessimism

GBD uses the same decision rule as KL-PBD, except that it uses the empirical mean h^j,Nj,t\widehat{h}_{j,N_{j,t}} instead of the lower confidence bound h¯j,t\underline{h}_{j,t}. Figure 16 shows, for every instance, the final regret of each of the 100100 runs against the run’s average deferral rate. For GBD the two are strongly negatively correlated, with correlation ρ∈[−.95,−.85]\rho\in[-.95,-.85] across the nine instances: runs that defer less accumulate more regret. This is the selective-feedback failure of greedy learning: an early optimistic estimate of the conditional accuracy of a level stops its deferrals, hence no more feedback for this level is received, and the estimate is never corrected. On Qwen2.5-0.5B NuminaMath, for instance, the deferral rate of GBD ranges from .15.15 to .31.31 and its regret from 1111 to 10,65810{,}658. KL-PBD+, which keeps deferring a level while its lower confidence bound is below the current threshold, shows neither the spread nor the correlation.
